item.title: On the Brutality of Amdahl's Law
item.description:
Following my 3-week visit to Berkeley as described here and featured by ACX here, I told various people I would write in detail why I didn’t stick around to work in AI safety. In this post, I will dance around one object-level disagreement with AI safety and rationalists: why I no longer believe in explosive world transformation due to ASI. There will eventually be follow-up pieces on more object-level arguments and meta-level arguments against AI safety, but I prefer for this post to be mostly self-contained and not explicitly about AI safety.

When I worked in theoretical physics research, I was constantly reminded that if I were just that much smarter and had read that many more papers, I would be able to make the right connection to solve the problem. You are always the bottleneck; it’s always a skill issue. So if you’ve spent the bulk of your conscious life honing your ability to manipulate the pure abstraction of math and computer code, it is staggering to watch the problems you wrestled with for months or years get blown away in hours. You are left wondering how quickly all of the other problems in the world will be resolved - all of disease perhaps? Why not all of biology? Why not all the secrets of the universe?

In December 2025 when Claude Code + Opus 4.5 first made agents feel extremely useful, I was concerned about the job market being obliterated, so I took out “insurance” on rapid-onset white-collar unemployment. Thankfully, those predictions about increasingly capable agents causing rapid economic and labor transformation have been very wrong.

And so the question is, why? Why does the world largely look the same outside of highly verifiable domains like software engineering and math, and even in software engineering, why are there still millions employed? Why are models which can beat humans on nearly all benchmarks and are provided at unbelievably low prices not causing large economic shockwaves?

If I had to summarize my current perspective on AI in a single sentence, it would be that “the world is far too slow” to see the high double-digit or more economic growth and seismic transformations in the economy as predicted by various essays from the rationalist blogo-instituto-sphere.

Amdahl’s Law

I suspect the reason I’ve felt less “capabilities whiplash” than my peers is that a lot of my experience is in experimental science where how smart you are is often not the actual bottleneck. To illustrate how enormous speedup in one component does not translate to enormous broader speedup due to other bottlenecks, let’s make a simple model:

If you have a process with some number of steps to be completed sequentially, each with rate i (ie each step takes time 1/to complete), your total rate is given by

If you send every rate but one to infinity, you are still left with

This is almost a trivial statement - your overall process is rate-limited by the slowest step, but it can be easily forgotten as you watch individual rates arc hyperexponentially upwards:

From the new METR report

More realistically, suppose you have some hierarchy of rates

where r₀ = a is the slowest and each successive rate is b times faster than the previous. The total rate of this hierarchy is

If you send the first m bottleneck rates to infinity, entirely eliminating each bottleneck, the new rate is

The point is that in hierarchically bottlenecked systems, even infinite speedup of the bottleneck results in a constant factor aggregate speedup. In order to see exponential aggregate speedup, you need explosive improvement at the current bottleneck over and over again. Overall progress is often brutally suppressed by this interplay between bottlenecks.

If during each time window you focus all of your efforts on accelerating the current bottleneck to ~infinity (or really just far beyond the next bottleneck or two), you see constant factor speedup. Repeated infinite individual factor speedup yields only exponential aggregate speedup.

To see diminishing returns, the intelligence curve need not flatten out; you just have to hit some other bottleneck. And so the question as it pertains to AI causing disruption in the world (for better and worse) is not “where is intelligence the rate-limiting step?” but “when intelligence becomes free, instant, and near-omniscient, what is the new rate-limiting step?” In computer science, this speedup analysis is known as Amdahl’s law and is used for understanding the limits of parallelism, but variants of it appear all across science.

Is Intelligence the Bottleneck?

I suspect the most common objection to the above analysis is that I am failing to imagine what ASI can accomplish. Instead of trying to abstractly rebut this, let’s look at a banal example of fairly bounded speedups even when you have access to ASI:

You’re the manager of a widget factory, and for some reason the defect rate has doubled in the past month. You’re able to use your process telemetry and slew of agents to figure out that tolerances during step 7 have blown out of the acceptable range. You haven’t changed anything about your process, so you have no idea what could be causing this. Four different precursors enter the process during step 7, but those haven’t changed either.

With the help of your ASI helper, you’re able to narrow down the possible causes of this specific kind of defect to inclusion of impurity X in material Y, but both precursors A and B contain Y. You reach out to the suppliers, but they shrug and say “sorry we haven’t changed anything”, so you need to diagnose which of these is the ultimate source. You order some tests on your new stock and the remnants of the old stock, and you find out that precursor A is causing your defect.

And now you have a decision to make: do you try to find a new supplier, remove the impurity yourself, or compensate for the impurity in other ways? You’ll need to run the tests on the new material or make a purification system or change your design. These all have tradeoffs and ASI will be able to help with all of these and pick the right one, but the fundamental problem here is that it takes time and money to install new systems to fix this problem. There is the time it takes to order new components, assemble them, install them. If you are integrating it into your telemetry system, you need all the sensors and wiring to feed into some database, and then finally you need to get your production up and running and make sure it’s all working.

The crux of AI disruption in my mind is these new bottlenecks which can be roughly split into two categories:

1. What are the speed limits in the world that intelligence does not accelerate?

The purely physical speed limits in the above example are things like sending out complicated tests to be run, ordering new components, installing new hardware into your factory, and manufacturing new widgets to verify your problem has been solved. There is a practical limit to how fast you can ship things across the country, and manufacturing steps involving chemical and biological processes have fundamental rates that can be on the order of days for things like culturing human cells and annealing metals.

Now suppose you also have humanoid robots to run your factory and install the new components, handling every step along the way. A very nontrivial percentage of the time in the above example is just dealing with the other companies, sending out materials for testing, having the new parts shipped to you, and installing the physical hardware and stress-testing it. This whole process could take a month in a current factory without superintelligence, but getting a 4x speedup to ~1 week seems about as fast as you can possibly go even with omniscient machines making perfect decisions at every step and working 24/7. At some point you’re quite literally bottlenecked on shipping time and physical throughput rate of tools in your factory.

There are also problems which are more or less solved - the steam engine has been around for 300 years, yet even fusion plants will likely end up turning a steam turbine. How many other problems in the world are in some sense solved and are very slow, expensive, and boring to improve? Other speed limits in the world are less physical but still important. What is the speed of regulation? What is the speed of political will?

It is worth disambiguating speedup and scale-up here. In something like the oil industry, a multitrillion dollar industry with enormous incentive to rapidly automate, it seems even a 3x speedup would be difficult. The oil comes out of the ground at some rate, is refined at some rate, and is transported at some rate, so the obvious answer if you want to double production is to parallelize everything and just have twice as much infrastructure. But massively expanding capacity in parallelization is itself a process that can be bottlenecked. Over the last year, strange scaling bottlenecks have looked like the monocrystalline turbine blades for natural gas plants and indium phosphide wafers for optical interconnects, and this has just been for running computers. If you believe in true industrial explosions, the demand for niche magnets and bearings and sensors and tool tips and alloys will explode, and any one of them can become the rate limiter.

2. What does it actually mean to be superintelligent in the presence of noise?

The more abstract speedup question is something like “could a superintelligence, given all the context of the situation, know right away that impurity X was the culprit and that it came from precursor A?” This would save you the time you spent running tests on A versus B and let you go straight to problem solving, but is this even possible? After all, the only thing that changed was the error bar in step 7.

In the aphorism “intelligence is compression”, there is a natural next question: What is the maximum amount of compression you can achieve in the real world? In order to realize that precursor A and not B had the impurity, you need to acquire 1 bit of information. Some bits, however, are unbelievably expensive to obtain and create a similar kind of Amdahl calculus. If key bits are orders of magnitude more expensive and slower to acquire (say, for example, long-term side effect analysis of new drugs on actual humans), these will set your overall rate.

It seems most people in AI consider the world to be far less noisy than it actually is because they mostly live in a world of flawlessly repeatable execution at staggering scale. Scaling experiments is as simple as spinning up more Docker containers, but the notion of superintelligence in domains like biology is ill-defined: There are large variations between nominally identical experiments, and the rate at which experiments produce informative bits is unfathomably low compared to anything in ML or verifiable like math. In other words, even information theory-optimal exploration of some problem landscape could be agonizingly slow if experiments are slow or noisy, let alone both. (To those who believe AI would be able to simulate any process accurately enough, it’s worth appreciating how poorly understood many multi-scale interactions are and how ground truth experimentation is often your best option. See also my blog post from April.)

Outlook

Intelligence is far from the only technology curve to go quasi-infinite in the last century and a half: The world electrified. The cost of communication has gone from couriers and weeks to ~free and gigabytes per second. Computers have made calculations which were once infeasible executable on a cheap computer near-instantly. Transportation costs have fallen by an order of magnitude. From 1880 to 2026, the share of the US workforce in agriculture fell from 51% to 1.2% as we were freed to work in other fields.

Yet through it all, we’ve seen nearly 150 years of 2% GDP per capita growth. These are all general-purpose technologies, so what needs to give for ASI to be that different?

item.title: Embryo selection and economic discounting
item.description:
My wife and I are planning to have children soon, and we will be using embryo selection to improve our family’s future well-being. Basically, the idea is that we can take a small sample of cells from each embryo, analyze their DNA, and use the genetic information to help choose which embryos we want to implant.

These days, polygenic scores are good at predicting risk for a lot of diseases, like cancer, heart disease, diabetes, schizophrenia, and Alzheimer’s. And companies like Herasight or Genomic Prediction often give an “embryo health score”[1] that takes an average of the predicted risk for each disease, weighted by how bad each disease is.

But how are those weights calculated? And can we do better?

Disability-adjusted life years

Diseases are bad in two ways: they can make you die, and they can make your life worse. The “disability-adjusted life year” (DALY) metric captures both of these, by combining years of life lost and years of reduced quality of life (using a factor between 0 and 1 to account for different subjective severity of disease states).[2]

Embryo selection companies, who compute polygenic scores for many different diseases, can add up the DALY burden of all the disease predictions for a given embryo. This gives an overall “embryo health score” that is a composite of these predictions.

A note on pleiotropy

Interestingly, many negative traits are genetically correlated with each other, so selecting against one selects against many. For example, our embryos that had a high schizophrenia risk also tended to have a high risk of bipolar. Pleiotropy (where one variant affects multiple traits) is often brought up in objections to embryo selection, e.g. “if you select for IQ, you might be selecting against health”, but in practice, mutations that make embryos less healthy will also generally hurt other traits.

Which diseases will be relevant in the future?

From as far back as 1950 until today, heart disease has been the biggest killer in the USA. And the DALY scores for embryos reflect this: heart disease has a strong weight.

But if a boy is born in 2027 with a high lifetime risk, he likely won’t develop any problems until middle age. Heart disease treatment will likely look very different in 2072! Therefore, we need to take into account future medical progress when weighing the badness of different diseases:

  • First, some things are already easily treatable. Statins lower cholesterol, and there are plenty of good medications for blood pressure. More recently, GLP1 drugs have made type 2 diabetes much less relevant. Some of these drugs are expensive today, but they will be generic in the future, and likely cheap and accessible.
  • On the other limb bud, any disease that is developmental in origin will not be treatable except by replacement of the affected structure. If something doesn’t form properly in the fetus, giving a drug to the adult won’t help.
  • However, organ replacement will probably be an option in 10-30 years, depending on the organ. This could include xenotransplantation or lab-grown “applied developmental biology” approaches. So things like heart disease and kidney disease will be curable, though this may be very expensive.
  • But nobody can get brain transplants.[3] Anything that affects the brain (depression, mental illness, neurodegeneration) will still be a huge problem. Very advanced technology may be able to replace the brain neuron-by-neuron, but I expect this to have the least progress compared to other diseases. Conditions that affect photoreception (e.g. colorblindness) will also be difficult to treat.
  • Cancer and autoimmune conditions are also not treatable with transplants, though emerging technologies will make treatment somewhat better.

Overall, I expect rapid medical progress in most areas over the next 50 years, especially given ongoing advances in AI. And if there’s a technological singularity, and everyone uploads their minds to run on silicon, then mental illnesses and personality disorders are the only thing that will matter!

Economic discounting

Leaving aside which conditions will be treatable in the future, the fact that some conditions have later average age of onset than others means that DALYs need to be adjusted for time-preference. For example, schizophrenia usually begins in early adulthood, whereas Alzheimer’s is a disease of old age. Selection for intelligence would have benefits at all stages of life.[4]

Embryo selection companies don’t take time-discounting into account for their embryo health scores.[5] However, health economists (e.g. in a study sponsored by the Gates Foundation) typically use a 3% annual discount rate. Personally, I think a 3% rate is on the low side: money invested today (instead of spent on embryo selection) would likely grow faster than that, especially given AI progress, and could be used to treat health conditions later in life. But I’ll use 3% in this post. Applied to the question of embryo selection, economic discounting means that late-onset conditions should be weighted less.

DALY adjustments

These are Herasight’s DALY numbers,[6] adjusted for 3% economic discounting, and further adjusted for future medical progress. I assume negligible progress in mental and neurological disorders, moderate progress in cancer and autoimmune, and faster progress in other categories (especially ones which are related to obesity/metabolic dysfunction).

Even after discounting, embryo selection is still worth it

For couples doing IVF, embryo selection (PGT) costs vary by provider but are often in the range of $500 per embryo.[7] IVF itself is much more expensive: we paid about $7500 per cycle at CNY, including costs of medication and travel, and other clinics are even more expensive. Side effects of hormone stimulation for egg retrieval also take a toll: based on my wife’s experience, I estimate that these side effects cause a loss of 0.025 DALY per IVF cycle.[8]

But all this is still much less expensive than the diseases that selection can prevent. As of 2026, one DALY is valued by the US government (HHS) as:

$726,000 … for analyses using a 3% discount rate, and $1,205,000 for analyses using a 7% discount rate[9]

Other US healthcare organizations place lower values on DALYs, often around $200,000. The difference is because the HHS number measures what people will pay to reduce their own risk of death, but other organizations are measuring cost-effectiveness of medical interventions relative to current treatment options.

The top embryo from our first IVF cycle had a non-discounted DALY gain of +1.35 years, and estimated IQ gain of +10 points, relative to our family average. Economic discounting and medical progress would shrink the DALY gain to +0.18 years, but this is still a gain of $133,000 for health and $151,000 for IQ, much more than we paid for the IVF and selection.

Of course we can’t be sure that our top embryo will successfully implant and develop to term, so we need to scale these numbers down to account for the chance we need to use our second-best or lower ranked embryos instead. In the end, being able to choose among the five embryos from our first cycle, rather than transferring them in random order, has an expected value of about $112,000.

Additional cycles run into diminishing returns, but I calculated that this point is reached for our family after 6 - 8 cycles.

Here, the optimal number of cycles is calculated as expected benefit (from health only, or health + IQ) with current Herasight predictors, minus the expected cost (direct financial cost and DALYs lost from IVF medication side effects).[10]

Our family is different from a typical family in several ways, including higher genetic risk of bipolar and schizophrenia, and younger than average age for IVF patients (meaning more embryos per cycle).

For typical families, embryo selection for health is worth it only at the highest estimates of DALY values. However, the picture changes when also considering IQ selection: typical families would come out ahead from doing at least 3 rounds of IVF, and interestingly, lower value placed on DALYs increases the optimal IVF cycle number, because the DALY cost of medication side effects becomes less relevant.

Conclusions

Given rate of progress in medicine, and economic growth, embryo selection to prevent early-onset disease is more important than selection to prevent late-onset disease. Prospective parents who are considering embryo selection should take this into account. Even with discounting, embryo selection for health+IQ still passes the cost-benefit analysis for most couples.

  1. ^

    “Embryo health score” is Genomic Prediction’s term; Herasight calls this “polygenic longevity index”.

  2. ^

    Calculation of these factors involves surveying patients and the general public about their preferences (e.g. would you rather live a year with blindness or with Crohn’s disease?), and involves a lot of statistics which I won’t get into here.

  3. ^

    If someone got a “brain transplant” it would actually be a “body transplant”.

  4. ^

    Economically, we can quantify this by the effect of IQ on future income. Grosse and Zhou estimated this as $10,600 per point (on the low end) in 2016 dollars. Adjusting for inflation, that would be about $15,000 today. As of this writing, Genomic Prediction does not offer intelligence selection but Herasight does.

  5. ^

    I asked a representative of Herasight about this, who said that they are considering adding an optional economic discounting feature in a future update, but haven’t formalized a framework yet.

  6. ^

    This combines years of life lost and years lived with disability. Herasight also uses different weights for male and female embryos, since women tend to live longer and some diseases affect women and men at different base rates. The table shows the average.

  7. ^

    Some companies like Herasight charge a fixed fee for analysis of any number of embryos, though biopsy fees also need to be paid to the IVF clinics.

  8. ^

    My wife’s experience was about as bad as a month of major depression for each cycle (30% loss of quality of life for a month). I’m very grateful for her going through this.

  9. ^

    They get these two different numbers by back-calculating from $14.1M as the statistical value of an average adult life based on surveys; i.e., an average American would be indifferent between losing $14,100 or having an 0.1% chance of death. Also, these numbers are technically QALYs not DALYs, though the difference is minor. Finally, for effects occurring in future years, they say to raise the value by 1.117% per year due to future real income growth, which partially offsets the discounting.

  10. ^

    These calculations depend on: the expected number of euploid embryos per cycle (3 for typical IVF patients, 5 for us), the live birth rate per euploid embryo (60% for typical IVF patients, 67% for us), and genetic risk (population average vs. our specific risks).

item.title: Slouching Towards Interpretability: Thinking About Computation in Neural Networks
item.description:
This post was written as part of the Iliad Fellowship, where I am mentored by Dmitry Vaintrob and collaborate with Brianna Grado-White. The initial inspiration came from conversation with Richard Ngo and Adrià Garriga-Alonso. To all of these my thanks.

I started writing this essay to share some thoughts on how to reconcile the idea of circuits with gradient descent. In doing this, I've come to change my perspective pretty substantially. The first half of this essay engages a Darwinian picture of circuits, but I think the central point - that we need a clearer ontology of computation in neural networks - holds without reference thereto.

Before, I was thinking about circuits as 'units of selection' - the kinds of things which engage in some gradient-hacking shenanigans to save themselves from gradient descent. I don't think this picture is unimportant or unhelpful, but I've come to think that it sidesteps the hard part of the problem - that the things the circuit Darwinism picture takes for granted are the confused parts, and I think therefore the more insightful to examine. I have gone from thinking "circuit Darwinism, but we need to formalize how to delineate the circuits" to "things that under circuit Darwinism seem like implementation details are actually the deep source of confusion, and we should treat these as the problem". I'll aim to convince you that this change in perspective is the right direction to head in.

I wrote this essay in three parts, plus what became a companion post.

  • The companion post is the 'Grimoire of Deep Learning' - things I think a mental model of wtf is happening in deep learning has to explain. While it informs later discussion, it is mostly separate from the present piece.
  • The first part offers two pictures of where circuits come from - "prune" and "precipitate" - and three conceptual problems I think a good theory of circuits has to solve.
  • The second part discusses some problems in specifying circuit Darwinism adequately - the model predicts very differently depending on what precisely we think circuits are, what the environment is, etc. and the naive guesses don't seem consistent.
  • In the third part, I'll outline an incomplete synthesis of how we get to 'defining circuits' - it takes the 'circuits live together, die together' intuition and works backwards: 'where do we look and how to find things that are selected together?'. This proto-synthesis has a lot of exciting connections to, i.a., neuroscience and dynamical-systems inference; for our purposes, the precise details are less the point than the fact that the richness of the problem should reveal how much confusion was hiding in 'implementation details'.
  • In the epilogue I envision a 'fundamental theory of interpretability' sufficient to argue for itself.

For highest value-to-engagement-demanded ratio, I recommend reading: part I (all parts), part II.e (the summary), the intro of part III, its summary III.d, and the Epilogue.

Part III has the most direct bearing on mechinterp and should be readable on its own, if that is your preference.

Contents

  • I. "Prune" or "Precipitate": Conceptual Problems in Specifying the Circuit Analogy
    • I.a. "Prune"
    • I.b. "Precipitate"
    • I.c. Conceptual Challenges
    • I.d. Grimoire of Deep Learning: an Invitation to Confusion
  • II. Problems with the Initial Circuit Ensemble
    • II.a. Infinite-Data Loss Implies a Decaying Circuit Population
    • II.b. Full-Batch GD (Mostly) Discredits Batch-Variance Selection
    • II.c. LLM Training Is Much Faster Than We'd Expect
    • II.d. It's Hard to Explain the Importance of Fresh Data
    • II.e. Summary
  • III. From the Neuron Up: Reservoir Computing, Coherent Sets, and Spectral Clustering
    • III.a. Reservoir Computing, Expansion Coding
    • III.b. Neurons Read Coherent Sets?
    • III.c. A Whiff of Unity: Activation Cells, Coherent Sets, and Spectral Clustering
    • III.d. Summary
  • Epilogue: Kritik of Fundamental Interpretability

I. "Prune" or "Precipitate": Conceptual Problems in Specifying the Circuit Analogy

In this first section, I'll frame the distinction by offering two visions of 'where circuits come from', and showing how this ostensible implementation detail ends up suggesting fundamentally different models. The first mental model I offer I call "Prune" - a naive circuit Darwinism that presupposes an 'initial circuit ensemble' amongst which competition occurs. The second I call "Precipitate", where circuits are 'grown' from the bottom up (roughly), as a crystal might be precipitated from solution.

I'll argue that the "Prune" picture requires a much greater specification of the analogy than we can yet give. "Precipitate" is an alternative I tried out to explain some empirical facts about deep learning and to connect to reservoir-computing models in neuroscience. It is less confused only insofar as it is less committal to the basic abstractions under study. Both are bottlenecked by our ability to deconfuse what exactly we mean by 'circuit'. I'll argue that the ability to characterise persistent structures is the central conceptual problem.

"Prune": the initial circuit ensemble

I.a. "Prune"

"Prune": This picture envisions the randomly initialized model as a tangled mass of circuits with arbitrary connections. It understands training as a process of pruning and re-allocating circuits and the connections between them. The reason it is useful to think this way is that it lets one straightforwardly apply the ideas of neural Darwinism - one imagines circuits competing for gradient, building gradient-barriers around themselves, etc. One can also then use the language of multi-level selection to talk about composition of circuits. I have written lovingly about how evolutionary-transitions theory could be used to think of composed circuits as coming to form a higher-level unit of selection.

When I think this way, I'm much more likely to think about looking for 'functional units' and their identification - it's more weight-space than activation-space in spirit. The most important posit of this theory is the 'initial circuit ensemble' - it tells us how 'dog ear' circuit wins over 'airplane nose' circuit, but not how either came about, nor how to identify or localise these circuits.

I.b. "Precipitate"

"Precipitate"

"Precipitate": This picture imagines the untrained network as a formless prima materia; development occurs mostly layerwise/stagewise, with many small (and nearly independent?) functional units. Circuits are grown, so the functional units are defined by their co-selection as much as anything. One reason to think this way is that it has connections to the biological theory of reservoir computing (for which v.i.), which describes how we can use random functions to do computation - the random functions are substrate not structure.

Because there are many libraries of random functions which we expect to be trainable to perform the same computation, this suggests we look instead at the dual - whatever the weights, similar programs should process data similarly: we ask what processing steps are done to the data, and trust that we can sort out who processed it later. This is the natural way to factor out the problem of irrelevant microstructure I mentioned in my previous essay. The spirit is to throw locality and modularity overboard, and find them a few weeks later where we least expect.

This picture has been useful to me less because it answers questions or better specifies the abstractions in question, and more because 'what if it's all slightly modified random functions' forces me to think much differently about looking for structure in the weights.

I.c. Conceptual Challenges

These models offered, I'll next outline three places where I think we need technical progress to achieve conceptual clarity - the right microscopes. These are things I think a good theory of circuits should incorporate, but for which we don't yet have good language. Of course, these are only the ones I currently have the wherewithal to see, as I am not yet a very incisive conceptual thinker when unguided by math - "who knows the words sees double" and all.

The first is scale-sensitive entity delineation ("at coarseness level 2.3, this weight is 90% part of circuitA and 1% part of circuitB and circuitC", "at coarseness level 2.3, circuitA and circuitB are 12% overlapping"). We need this because neural networks are messy, so obviously we should be asking 'scalar' questions instead of binary 'yes/no', and because circuits should compose, we need a scale parameter to set what 'size' of circuit we're looking for.

The second is a notion of similarity between implementations of a computation - ideally general enough that we could compare Mamba, LSTM and GPT implementations of 'the same circuit' ("the Mamba and the LSTM both learned grade-school multiplication, but the GPT learned Karatsuba multiplication" h/t Erez Abrams). This is necessary to solve the "irrelevant microstructure" problem mentioned earlier - we want to 'factor out' the spurious implementation details.

Third and finally is a notion of expressivity as a resource. The idea here is that ReLU (or whatever) is a very simple function. It is presumably the case that if we had far more expressive neural layers (e.g. ones which solve convex optimization problems), we should expect computation to be organized very differently. One idea I have considered recently is what it would look like for neural networks to be bottlenecked by computational expressivity rather than a concept/neuron ratio à la superposition. In reservoir computing (v.i.), neuron count is the number of pulls you get at the random-function slot machine - more neurons means larger repertoire of computations rather than more storage. Of the three problems outlined here, this is the one which I've thought least about.

To paraleptically mention the mathematics I've been using to identify (as opposed to solve, lol) these problems: I think of entity-delineation through the lens of spectral clustering and coherent structures. Computation-similarity I have been thinking about with realization theory and Hankel methods. Expressivity-as-resource I have been thinking about through Galerkin projections of the Koopman operator.

(no, Claude didn't write that; I really am just this way...:') ).

I.d. Grimoire of Deep Learning: an Invitation to Confusion

In early drafts of this post I had a big list of surprising findings about how deep learning works (which I expect to be probably directionally correct) which I think any theory has to reckon with. I've instead broken this out to a separate post. The main ideas are summarized here:

  • There's probably a qualitative difference between "early" and "late" training, with early training being more 'formative' than late training. Tentatively, early training sees 'representation formation', while late training 'sharpens' these representations.
  • Lots of things appear to be architecture independent in a meaningful way, perhaps including even the overall structure of the learned representation. I forget who said this, but I've heard it said that "talking to Claude is talking to its training data".
  • Models are robust to really strange kinds of ablations, and this makes it hard to imagine a layer as secretly implementing one step of a boolean circuit. There's probably an implicit tradeoff between 'learning new computations' and 'denoising or becoming more confident in old ones'.
  • Gradient flow (with no noise etc.) at least kinda works, so whatever our explanation is, it should at least kinda work if we assume that training can never cross a loss barrier.

II. Problems with the Initial Circuit Ensemble

In this section, I'll talk about some problems with a strong form of circuit Darwinism which I've dubbed the 'initial circuit ensemble'. These 'problems' will all end with the conclusion "that's fine - in fact we can fix it by making one of three plausible simple assumptions about the precise analogy we're making to neural networks". My thesis here is that we can't yet make the Darwinian analogy precise enough to think clearly with it; figuring out 'what circuits are' is the core conceptual and technical problem.

We will take the 'initial circuit ensemble model' to have two important propositions:

  • the network is conceived of as being made entirely of circuits
  • these circuits are present from initialisation, or we can otherwise take for granted their existence

Problems with the initial circuit ensemble:

  • the infinite-data, finite-parameter loss limits the total amount of selection; squaring this with adaptation is hard
  • full-batch training works far better than would be expected by selection-for-selectability arguments
  • LLM training takes place in extremely few steps compared to what we'd expect from evolution, especially if we think of grokking as a baseline
  • the theory cannot explain the importance of fresh vs. stale data, and in fact selection-for-selectability arguments suggest the opposite effect.

Put another way, we're confused about what the 'population' is, how circuits adapt, die, or replenish, what 'the environment' is, and what the right unit of time is - the naive identifications mostly don't work.

I'll also add that there are many effects which I think are important discussed in the companion post which our underspecified circuit Darwinism just can't engage with usefully, especially the early-/late-training distinction.

II.a. Infinite-Data Loss Implies a Decaying Circuit Population

Here I'll argue that we can only explain the infinite-data loss by positing a decaying effective-population of circuits - otherwise circuit Darwinism predicts continued improvement from endogenous competition. [1]

Consider the Chinchilla scaling law

with the loss, the parameter count, and the amount of data.

We see that for infinite data, there remains a contribution from the number of parameters. By default, for fixed circuit size, the number of parameters is something like the number of parallel selection events, and so should set the rate of competition, but have no definite effect on its outcome.

I think the simplest explanation for this (though it has other problems matching the scaling law!) would be to imagine that the circuit population decreases over time (perhaps as circuits aggregate into bigger units, or are simply selected away) - eventually, there are circuits left and no further selection can occur. This lets us predict an -dependent saturation. It also predicts that the rate of selective progress should decrease as does, but I'm not comfortable equating that to loss-reduction and don't have a better guess.

This isn't the end of the world, but we now enter the territory of having to think about circuits dying vs being absorbed, and how the size of circuits should change over time, and whether they eat the parameters that would otherwise give rise to new circuits - these are things that could happen, and it would be useful to think of them in Darwinian terms - the problem is that we're expanding the number of alternative things our model can predict while we have no way of measuring or identifying which of those things actually win out.

That is to say: not a dunk on circuit Darwinism - but a point for needing more microscopic understanding of variation so we can get the rules of the game straight.

II.b. Full-Batch GD (Mostly) Discredits Batch-Variance Selection

Circuit Darwinism imagines that circuits compete with one another - and in particular we should hope that there is some mechanism by which 'more general' circuits outcompete 'less general' ones, so that we can explain generalization.

One of the ways I liked to explain this was by positing that, imagining we have several circuits competing to fulfill the same function, we should expect the general one to have a low per-sample gradient, while the more memorize-y one might depend on a precarious balancing of positive and negative pulls from samples in a given batch. This batch-variance selection corresponds schematically to the Bergstrom–Lachmann effective penalty for having a fitness which varies.

This seems to be discredited by the fact that full-batch GD works at least somewhat meaningfully (see companion post) in image and language models. Of note is that the Nanda grokking paper also uses full-batch - as best I can tell, grokking relies on the regularization to work, not batch noise.

To be clear, other types of things like EoS could select to prefer less noisy circuits, but the hope of batch-variance selection was that we could imagine this as leading to generalization by being like 'test the organism in many environments'. We certainly have 'make this organism robust to mutation' effects still, but just in a generic not-related-to-environment way. It becomes harder to imagine selection-for-selectability occurring, which I've hitherto understood as synonymous with 'generalization' in Darwinism.

There are of course other ways we could imagine selection for generalizable circuits occurring, perhaps because more generalizable circuits produce outputs which are 'useful to more downstream tasks' or something like this, but the fact that batch noise seems to be merely important rather than the sine qua non of generalizability makes it hard to think of batch-noise as environment variation as generalization-pressure.

This shouldn't be overstated: gradient flow only works if you try really hard to make it - full-batch GD is pathological but still works within reason. This means we need a theory that at least kinda works without selection-for-selectability, at least in the sense I had imagined it.

II.c. LLM Training Is Much Faster Than We'd Expect

Next I'll argue that the number of optimization steps in frontier LLM training runs makes it implausible that Darwinian competition is the best description of what is occurring. The numbers here are all extremely sus - I tried to save you the thirty footnotes that would add caveats - but I'm confident in the overall "deep learning very fast, evolution very slow - needs explanation".

First note that the grokking experiments in the Nanda paper show grokking time on the order of 5k epochs (iiuc getting grokking requires a bit of fiddlin' with the parameters, so cum grano salis). If you squint, TMoS takes about the same [2] , plus-or-minus an OOM.

More substantively: a quick google says training GPT-3 took about 100k steps. Presumably this varies by several OOMs for frontier models - this is just an existence proof. If we imagine grokking as the prototypical "competition between circuits selects for the more general one" event at 5k steps, GPT-3 gets twenty 'rounds' of selection.

Compare this to Haldane's limit, which suggests that a population can manage only about one adaptive substitution per 300 generations. Though it does violence to our analogy between LLMs and population genetics, ~2M params per step (175B params / ~94k steps) vs. 100 steps per param is enough OOMs to make the qualitative point - evolution is slow.

Let's do another egregiously simple comparison to ensure that anyone that knows anything hates me: suppose the human brain has 100T params (100B neurons and 1k synapses per), with a tick time of 100ms - fixing 2M params per step means seconds - 2 months, give or take some OOMs, lol. So in terms of train time "brain is closer to LLMs than evolution".

Again, this is easily patched by, say, talking about the number of parallel queries, or taking the 2M parameters fixed to mean like '1 parameter per circuit', etc.

But then we again enter the frustrating realm of needing to specify very precise details that we don't have the ability to check - 'is competition between all the circuits at once? or in small groups doing similar functions?'.

For my purposes, a weaker, safer version of this claim is fine: we're confused about how to think about the time-scales on which circuits compete and adapt.

II.d. It's Hard to Explain the Importance of Fresh Data

Finally, I think the thing that's hardest to explain under circuit Darwinism is the importance of fresh data.

Evolution doesn't really have a role for something like the amount of data - we only get to smuggle it in by assuming compute-optimality and treating it as 'time'. If we try to think of as the 'amount of unique environments' our little tamagotchi circuits are selected under, one can recover a prediction that the final loss should depend on , but there's no way to reconcile this with the fact that the loss reduction falls to nearly zero after ~16 epochs.

My favorite mechanism for how you could get generalization from circuit Darwinism is 'selection for selectability' (S4S) - it is precisely this repeated oscillation of the environment that drives selection-for-selectability (related to generalization), and this effect is parametrically small compared to instantaneous selection, so we would predict that many epochs of training would be needed to saturate the usefulness of data. We could have said that ackshually the environment fluctuation is batch-noise, but as I argued above this seems wrong too.

So we're confused about how exactly to think about 'environment variation' over time. A blind spot I haven't talked about at all is that we can't usefully address the comparative importance of endogenous competition vs environment change for adaptation.

II.e. Summary

I've argued that thinking usefully of circuit Darwinism requires us to be much more specific about the detailed ontology of the theory than we are ready to be.

Scaling laws imply a finite reservoir of variation on which selection can occur, so we have to provide an account for how we can get enough 'interesting' variation that Darwinism is useful while also predicting its limitedness.

We can't understand batch-noise or epochs of training as directly representing environmental variation in the way that lets us get selection-for-selectability effects, so it would have to come from some other unit of time.

Finally, training an LLM takes extremely few steps. Selection-for-selectability (which my mental model hitherto identified with generalization) is parametrically slow - e.g. if 'environments' were different kinds of documents for an LLM, it would scale with the number of documents rather than tokens. We need to drop S4S or posit that the correct 'unit of time' isn't the optimizer step.

In sum, to think usefully about any kind of circuits competing or doing interesting Darwinian stuff, we need to get much more precise about the analogy, and we simply don't have precise enough definitions to make the predictions that would test between these different versions of the model.

This section is in essence an argument that 'wtf is a circuit' is the core confusion, conceptually and technically, rather than an implementation detail.

Onwards!

III. From the Neuron Up: Reservoir Computing, Coherent Sets, and Spectral Clustering

In this section I'll talk about two threads that have fed into my thinking about how we can talk about functional units arising in LLMs.

First I'll discuss two related ideas from neuroscience, 'reservoir computing' and 'expansion coding'. Then I'll relate this to kernel learning on random functions - we'll see that 'real learning' lives in the changing of these random functions, which corresponds to a network updating its inductive biases.

Next I'll change tack and present a toy model of a neuron that learns to predict its next input, and relate this to a more general technique called spectral clustering. This motivates looking at activations and asking how we can think about the network 'treating some group of data points the same' - as a warmup for finding functional groupings like circuits.

I'll then draw on an empirical observation about LLM activations to motivate a relaxed version of spectral clustering in activation-space. The idea is to imagine coherent sets of activations as coarse-grained 'computational states'. If circuits 'live together, die together', these 'computational states' are things that are 'processed together'. A work in progress.

Two things to note: first, there's a bit of a jump after part a - I don't know how to connect the ideas in this part yet, but they have been very influential to my mental models. Second, in III.c I'll write about how I've been thinking about this theory in activation-space. This post outlines conceptual problems to activation-space interpretability (though I think these mostly do not apply for my purposes). Please do not feel deceived - I too want a theory of circuits, and hope to develop the theory to get us back to weight-space++ soon.

III.a. Reservoir Computing, Expansion Coding

Reservoir computing is a model in neuroscience that attempts to explain how a big ol' soup of randomly connected neurons can usefully store and retrieve patterns. This YouTube video describes it well. The short of it is that each neuron is essentially a random function (the soup's weights are assumed fixed, and they're all recurrent-y, not layerwise); then each pattern you want to learn is a linear readout of the neurons. It seems part of the hippocampus and fly olfactory bulbs do something like this!

This turns out to be more-or-less equivalent to kernel learning with random features in ML! Both learn , with your random functions (in ML these are probably vectors, but in reservoir computing they're functions of time). This is cool! Random-feature kernel learning feels pretty primitive to us in the deep learning age - the first main point here is that we can show that learning is really possible if you just take a linear readout on sufficient amounts of random bullshit - i.e., there is no circuit-like structure anywhere, and we can still do something useful.

The second point is more macro-level. We know that random-feature learning has scaling laws AND we know that for a technical definition of 'learn', these kernel learners do not 'learn'. In particular, we can understand kernel methods as never updating their 'inductive biases', while other methods do. See The Principles of Deep Learning Theory (ch. 10–11) for this formulation of inductive bias. It is possible to get scaling laws while definitely not learning, and neuron soup just about does this.

A close-by idea I've found useful is 'expansion coding'. This is a coding scheme where computation is done primarily by computing a bunch of random functions of your inputs, and hoping one of them is useful. I.e., it's basically the same thing as above just with less contextual baggage. On this picture, you compute by computing enough random functions that hopefully one of them is at least sorta doing XOR, then just picking that one.

Insofar as representational superposition / sparse-sensing are what you should do when you have many more concepts than neurons, expansion coding is kiiiinda opposite - it's what you should do if computational expressivity is super limited but you have neurons out the wazoo.

In the companion post, we talked about NTK fitting-vs-rotation as being one way of thinking about 'early' and 'late' training being very different. Here we can note that reservoir-computing is approximately the same as the NTK regime. What we want is a story that interpolates from "fitting random functions" to "memorizing n-grams" to "simulating the universe".

I'll also gesture noncommittally to the (contested) lottery-ticket hypothesis - the idea of which is that you can usually find a tiny sub-network inside your network such that if you rewind training and prune everything else, only training that network suffices to get you most of the loss-reduction. This suggests that there's some grounds to imagine starting with a big bag of random functions and modifying them.

I'm not confident in this, but I think we have not thought enough about what it would look like for networks to be bottlenecked by computational expressivity rather than representation capacity.

The two models above have been influential in my thinking. In the next sections I'll try to get much more specific and explain how we might think of neurons as 'detectors of coherent sets' - I apologize that I can't yet draw a more direct connection between these two halves of the picture, but hopefully each is informative :)

III.b. Neurons Read Coherent Sets?

Back in the good old days, we thought a lot about 'receptive fields' of neurons - what kinds of things activate them? Here's one trivial idea: "the input weights of a neuron divide input-space into regions, and the neuron's activation is a scalar membership score for that region; then in proportion to that membership, the input-activation gets nudged in a direction fixed by the neuron's output-weights".

Now without going too much into detail about my special interest [3] , there is a way to see this trivial observation from a very different angle. In this paper, they analyse a neuron which reads a single scalar input signal and predicts . Roughly, the should come from the singular vectors of the time-evolution matrix and go 'ping' when it sees a similar pattern - morally, the neuron gets a vector of inputs and goes ping when that vector is in a coherent set.

In case the math lost you, the one-liner: the receptive field of a neuron is a coherent set of its input-space.

While I am trying very hard to write no additional math about my favorite thing in the world, I had already drawn Niels the neuron teaching coherent set detection when I decided to cut down the math. Niels, presumably in collaboration with your LLM, explains:

Niels the Neuron explains how the SVD of the delay-embedding Hankel matrix is spectral clustering on input-patterns; after Pughe-Sanford et al. 2025

These coherent sets are important to us neuron-enjoyers because they are the sets which are in some sense the most predictive of future state - they're an approximation to the optimal coarse-graining, forgetting as much microscopic detail as possible (where in the set the point was) while remaining maximally useful for predicting the future macroscopic state (i.e., the particle is still in the set and the set hasn't much changed shape).

Spectral clustering triptych: similarity-graph → eigenproblem → partition the thing into different regions

Btw, as in the picture, 'spectral clustering' is when you take some graph, find eigenfunctions on it, and then use those eigenfunctions to 'segment' it into clusters - I mention this later, but I consider this admissible as an interpretability technique because it's essentially an SVD. It is 'the most complicated thing that still counts', because SVDs are great, so the argument reduces to arguing that you're SVD-ing the right thing.

III.c. A Whiff of Unity: Activation Cells, Coherent Sets, and Spectral Clustering

The dream of interpretability is to be given a knob, call it , such that making it very small lets you resolve very coarse structure very cheaply, and that, tuning it up, you can resolve finer structure at increasing computational cost. Ideally, you can focus your efforts on a particular behaviour rather than the whole model, and spend your limited computational power analysing particularly important computations (presumably of the alignment flavour).

My collaborator Brianna Grado-White and I have spent the last few months, i.a., looking at the activation cells in LLMs. These are Voronoi-like cells in activation-space such that points in the same cell are treated in essentially the same way by the network. Our aim has been to figure out if we can understand these as discrete states of some computation - if so, we could reduce the model to a table of transition rules (presumably not perfectly!), which would then be the natural thing to analyse.

Figure 1 from Janiak et al.: Voronoi-cell-like structure in the residual stream of LLMs

In part because of tractability issues, in part because of theoretical connections between computation identification and Hankel methods, and in part pursuing the intuition that we should be looking at 'points the network treats the same' more macroscopically, we're working on developing a technique which analyses clusters of data-points building on this perspective.

Label propagation on a similarity graph of MNIST digits; from this paper. I'm imagining that LLM activation cells are ~ isolated subcomponents of this graph, with training points labeled.

Activation cells are groups of points the network 'treats similarly'; old ML has a family of methods called label propagation where it'll propagate the labels of known data-points to unknown ones through a similarity graph.

You can sorta-kinda-don't-think-too-hard-about-it understand the activation cells as perfectly-isolated groups of points - training points inside a cell are labeled, and any test-points in the cell are connected up to it.

The core idea is that we can do a much more macroscopic version of this by approximating the similarity graph. There are plenty of design choices to be made here, but this turns out, morally, to be spectral clustering!

I've outlined the idea in this image. In this case, we use a 'dynamic similarity' measuring how points move between layers, rather than their similarity at a given layer.

Coherent sets of activations are those the network 'treats the same' between some specified layers L' → L

While I'm trying to practice writing without math, I'm well aware that "I drew it on the whiteboard" strains credibility if you don't know me well enough to know that I have cut >1000 words on Hankel matrices from drafts of this post. As bona fides, here's a teaser of the method applied to ResNet18+CIFAR10. Preliminary, working on the writeup, but proof of concept.

Here we fit data-points into 4 coherent sets based on how they move through the first ~half of the network at t=2500 steps; we color the corresponding points for all other times and layers. The left is just UMAPs of the activations. The right is class composition and representative images of the four coherent sets.

Eyeballing, it seems to be ~separating things by background colour. Once I earn it, the desired interpretation is something like "at time t=2500, at the resolution scale of 4 coherent sets, the first half of the network seems to treat points similarly according to their background colour". Again, work in progress.

III.d. Summary

Okay so in this section I've covered two big ideas: first, what reservoir computing has to tell us about how random neural networks can work (and how this is like NTK learning) and what it might look like for a network to be bottlenecked by computation rather than by representation; second, how we can think of the natural operation of neurons as spectral clustering, and how spectral clustering and coherent structures are a natural language for characterising how a neural network treats data en masse.

I think expansion coding and reservoir computing are important as, in spirit, an alternative perspective to the superposition hypothesis. Schematically, superposition imagines networks are bottlenecked in the number of concepts they can represent. There are good theories of 'computation-in-superposition', but I've found myself wanting a model that centers 'computational expressivity' as the bottleneck. Expansion-coding is, i.a., a story of how neural networks can work if neurons are cheap but computation difficult or inexpressive. I like it mainly because this is very contiguous with what we know to be the case for NTK-regime-learning. I'm not sure how to make it more substantive or bridge to the coherent structures bit yet.

The coherent structures / spectral clustering thing is much more substantial as a framework for thinking about what neurons are doing and how they encode information. In particular, my most curmudgeonly fundamental-interp-research opinion is that the only thing that is truly interpretable is an SVD, so we need to find the right SVD, and we'll call this spectral clustering. [4] This family of ideas makes me excited by the amount of things it's connected to - predictive state representations, realization theory, approximation of automata... Claude dared me to add quantum channel metrology lol.

[edited by GPT]

The end goal has always been to find the mathematical object which tells us what the network's ontology is. I'm excited to think about this more!

Epilogue: Kritik of Fundamental Interpretability

I will close by reflecting on my aims and vision for a 'fundamental theory of interpretability'. Briefly, and then with elaboration:

A fundamental theory of interpretability must be complete enough to justify its ontology and argue for its own completeness.

John Wentworth has an excellent post about Shannon's contribution to cryptography: before we knew what mutual information was, people did hacky things like making sure encrypted text had zero correlation with the plaintext, but would pikachu surprise face when you could hack their cypher by using information stored in higher order correlations. The correct answer is of course to zero out the mutual information, which captures all such effects.

Shannon did not postulate some quantity and prove that it fortuitously solves the problem of encryption - Shannon invented the language by which we know what it means for an encryption to be perfect. The argument that mutual information is the correct quantity to evaluate encryption is inextricable from the argument for inventing mutual information at all - perfection by design!

This is what I want from a theory of interpretability - the theory must be able to justify its ontology independently of the theory's practical results, and must be sufficiently complete to argue for its completeness.

Practically, this is why the river of random math and spectral clustering and Hankel matrices and... - not a flailing for things to throw at the wall, but because I am groping after the combination of ontology and mathematical tools sufficient to argue for itself.

To be useful for superalignment - modulo dropping all your chips on Big Orange 6 and spinning the wheel - we must have an interpretability which we have the right to expect works. This is the thing I want from a 'fundamental theory of interpretability'.

It is a grand and humbling thing to stand confused in the shadow of this last Deep Mystery. For this, and for those who stand with me, I am grateful beyond words.

"All processes that are stable we shall predict. All processes that are unstable we shall control." — John von Neumann (attributed by Freeman Dyson)

I had it find most of the links and handle most of the markdown formatting. I specified almost all linked items; those Claude suggested I read before including. There should be ~0 LLM-written prose in this post. GPT badly edited the boss-baby meme, lol.

  1. more accurately, Darwinism more readily talks of relative proportions of a phenotype rather than its absolute numbers, so it doesn't often say anything about a trend in 'overall' fitness, which is a bit more the domain of population ecology. ↩︎

  2. I had codex do some sanity checks on this and it seems to take O(10k) steps, though if you use Adam instead of SGD it takes ~100 steps. This remained roughly true at the sparsity ratio implicit in GemmaScope (71 active of 16k = 0.4% = 7x compression). Surprisingly, the time-to-learn is ~constant at fixed compression-ratio (num_inputs per hidden-layer neuron) - suggesting learning rate is the relevant bottleneck to superposition rather than capacity. While we know SGD doesn't work on transformers, lest we take this as evidence of the necessity of superposition, the Adam-mini paper (building on Zhang et al.) shows this is due to component heterogeneity, and fixing a component-wise learning rate suffices to train. If you like, you're welcome to consider the weakened argument that we're confused about how to think about generation-time in the Darwinian analogy. ↩︎

item.title: Be Grateful in Spite of Your Suffering
item.description:
I've been in tremendous pain lately. My body is shutting down. I haven't slept properly in months. I've lost 15lbs because my appetite disappeared. Yet, throughout it all, I'm trying to remember to be grateful in spite of my suffering.

When life flips the coin of fate and it lands on the side of darkness, all I want to do is protest, to shake my fist at God and shout, “Why, why, why hath thou forsaken me?” And when my cries go unanswered, and I'm left at the bottom of an abyss shivering and shaking to stay warm, I try to remember that with every darkness that visits me, if I find the strength and courage even when I'm at the end of my rope, I can flip over the coin of fate and find the sliver of light dimly shining and attempting to pierce the darkness. I try to remember to be grateful in spite of my suffering.

Swords are made by putting them through fire and then beating them relentlessly. Unrefined chunks of iron ore, transformed into sleek and refined blades, capable of cutting through those who dare to stand in its way. When I'm standing in the fire alone, being charred alive, my screams falling on deaf ears, I try to remember that burned skin grows back, and the scars are a reminder of the time that I stood in flames and endured the pain. I try to remember to be grateful in spite of my suffering.

In trying times, I find great comfort in the words of those who have come before me, from those who have walked through the valley of pain and emerged on the other side beaten, bruised, and limping, but still alive. The coldness of the abyss below softly whispers to me that a shortcut to warmth is just on the other side, enticing me to the edge of darkness, daring me to leap. With the rhythmic beating of a drum, calling me closer to the edge, this proverb is echoing in my mind: “The child who is not embraced by the village will burn it down to feel its warmth.” Yes, warmth. I so desperately want to escape this biting, gnawing cold. Shivering, on the verge of collapse, another thought descends from above, a quote from Henry David Thoreau: “The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation.” Yes, quiet desperation, as the cold consumes me from the outside in. But then, from above, another thought: a reminder that that's not the full quote. In full it reads: “The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation. They honestly think there is no choice left. But alert and healthy natures remember that the sun rose clear. It is never too late to give up our prejudices.” And with that, collapsed and shivering in the unending cold, the icy fog occluding the sun parted, and a sliver of light from above descended and kissed my cold and brittle cheek. The glimmer of light, with its soft and subtle warmth, stirred within me a strength that had lain dormant deep inside me. Channeling that strength, and the warmth that deigned to visit me, I rose again. Stumbling through the valley of pain with nothing but a sliver of light to guide me through the fog, I try to remember to be grateful in spite of my suffering.

item.title: Should prices sum to $1 for undecidable sentences?
item.description:
Previously: Logical Share Splitting, Logical Share Splitting for Intuitionists

Recap:

This series is about prediction markets for mathematics.

Imagine a game where players trade tickets with mathematical sentences written on them. A ticket is redeemable for $1 if you can demonstrate a proof of the sentence written on it. (A ticket is like a prediction market share in that sentence.) In this system, it's also allowable to exchange a ticket for another ticket with a logically equivalent sentence written on it, if you can demonstrate a proof of that logical equivalence.

(Actually, this rule can be made even more permissive if we like: It's allowable to exchange an ticket for a ticket if . That way if your newly obtained ticket is worth anything, we know that the ticket would have been worth at least as much, and therefore your wealth either stayed the same or declined. As ticket Czars, this is very reassuring to us, because we certainly would not want for you to have gained wealth at our own expense. That kind of thing is supposed to be reserved for your interactions with other traders. This operation is called irreversible exchange, because once performed, it can't generally be undone.)

By issuing tickets in a given sentence for a price of less than $1, you can thus put bounties on mathematical theorems. People can buy the tickets for your lower price and sell them for $1, so long as they can prove the theorem.

This ticket-trading system functions as prediction market for mathematics. The price of a sentence corresponds to what people think the chance is that a proof will be found for it.

For completeness, we have to include a somewhat surprising trading rule into this system: Tickets with sentences are tradable (in either direction) for tickets with sentences . This rule is introduced in the original logical share splitting post linked above.

The second post notes that, since a real implementation of this ticket system would involve using an automatic formal proof checker to verify submitted proofs, we should probably pay some attention to how an automatic proof checker actually works. And these proof checkers are constructive by nature. In particular, this means that they don't naturally have the Law of Excluded Middle. Proof checkers can still be used to do classical logic, simply by adding the Law of Excluded Middle as an additional axiom. But they mesh most naturally with intuitionist logic.

In classical logic, there are many equivalent forms of the logical share splitting operation. For example, trading for $ \neg(B \Rightarrow A), A \Rightarrow B$. But, as the second post points out:

  1. These classically equivalent rules can be intuitionistically distinct. And of these distinct rules, most of them are invalid. The original rule where we trade for remains valid. Therefore we should use that one.

  2. Because of the property of intuitionist logic that the only way to prove is to provide a proof of or a proof of , there is a sense in which logical share splitting is more valid under intuitionist logic than otherwise. Under classical logic, a proof of may be possible, without any ability to prove or individually. So a trader who owns tickets with and that would be worthless on their own due to the lack of proofs, could perform logical share splitting to obtain and redeem that ticket. This would be an instance of logical share splitting allowing a trade of a valuable ticket for a value-less one. The intuitionist version prevents this.

  3. Splitting up the work of writing proofs between multiple minimally-coordinated parties remains possible. However, it becomes somewhat less elegant; and somewhat more coordination is required.

So that was parts 1 and 2.

I've since managed to clean up the situation a bit more, reducing the amount of inter-party coordination needed back to the baseline from part 1. So in this post, I'll describe how to do that. We keep the basic framework of intuitionist logical share splitting, but for convenience build in a way of handling the classical logic side of things too.

Part 3: The Complement and Living in Both Worlds

The basic idea is that, while we do not have (the law of excluded middle) in general, we will introduce a weaker version of it. We need to have two kinds of negation. The first kind, , we are already familiar with. The second kind is distinct and new. We will call it "complement" instead of "negation". We write the complement of as . The point of the complement is that, while we do not have , we do have . Some version of the law of excluded middle holds for the complement.

Axioms for the Complement

There are two axioms:

  • (complement excluded middle)

  • (complement contravariance)

Advantages

Working in a system with both negation and complements lets us get the best of both worlds. We have the standard negation of intuitionist logic, and also a complement, that means that in some sense and cover all possibilities.

In the ticket trading system, we expect things with proofs to ultimately end up being worth $1. But it is not very rare at all for some sentences to be neither provable nor disprovable.
