item.title: Transcript: Yudkowsky & Irving debate scalable oversight
item.description:
In August 2026 Eliezer Yudkowsky and Geoffrey Irving had a 90-minute debate at the ILIAD III Conference. You can watch the "Fixed Audio"-version on YouTube. They first identify their disagreements like How hard is superalignment? and discuss the theory of impact of Irving's new organization Resolution. They then go into depth on scalable oversight.

Epistemic Effort: I transcribed the audio using 5 services and merged those using Claude Fable 5.1. Then I spent ~6 hours carefully reviewing and editing the transcript. (I also added links and [disagreement which they indicated non-verbally]. Subheadings by Claude Fable 5.2.)

Introductions

Yudkowsky [00:00]: Hi, I'm Eliezer, well-known Harry Potter fan fiction author. [cheering] [laughter]

Irving [00:10]: I'm Geoffrey Irving. I'm now the chief scientist at Resolution. I was at, for better or worse, various labs before, and also AISI.

Audience member: And Pixar.

Irving: And Pixar. [laughter]

Survey of disagreements

Yudkowsky: So we're going to try to resolve all of our open disagreements over the course of the next hour. [laughter] An impossible task, but not as impossible as some, really. [laughter] So I would propose that we maybe take turns stating beliefs, that we suspect the other might disagree with, that we ourselves hold. And then this [lowers his hand to the floor] is very low disagreement, and this [holds his hand up high] is very high disagreement.

And so we can do a quick survey of the field before we actually go depth first into anything.

Irving: Sounds great.

How hard is superalignment?

Yudkowsky: All right. I suspect that we have a disagreement about how difficult alignment is exactly. And in particular, I expect that superalignment is kind of beyond the reach of current human institutions or their close neighbors.

Irving: Here. Or sorry, here. [Irving indicates high disagreement] I think there's a question. This is maybe slightly related, but just to say it even anyways. I think it's plausible that a relatively small number of modifications to current training is sufficient. Plausible does not mean that high probability, but plausible enough to try with that theory of impact in mind. [Yudkowsky indicates very high disagreement] [laughter]

Yudkowsky: Where plausible enough to try is doing a bunch of work there. If you're like, in principle, it's a small number of modifications, I'm like over here. [Yudkowsky indicates low disagreement] And if you're like, we can figure out those modifications, then I'm up over here. [Yudkowsky indicates very high disagreement]

Irving: Well, yeah, in between those two. I think the kind of aggregate change one could make with this kind of theory is, on total effect, low tens of percent to a few percent maybe is what I would say is overall change in we all die factor.

Yudkowsky: I suspect that current gradient descent, reinforcement learning-based techniques are tending to produce pretty alien psychology that makes alignment not easy. [Irving indicates medium disagreement]

Irving: I feel like I don't disagree with that one very much. I [3 words unintelligible] do think, though, that maybe this is an important thing to say. I think the alignment solutions we will need— that we could plausibly get in time to make a difference on current trajectories will be able to treat gradient descent-based models that learn heuristics in strange ways relatively generically without understanding exactly how those heuristics emerge. [Yudkowsky indicates medium disagreement]

Yudkowsky: Is my degree of disagreement with, like, if we can understand the heuristics relatively generically or something, like, half true, half not true or? According to me.

Irving: I guess it's more that I think that— well, we'll get into details there, but to say it briefly, I think we need to have some knowledge of how heuristics emerge from a gradient descent. But I think I expect us to have ideas and toy models and cartoon pictures of this process and for it to not be very precise.

And then if your intervention to alignment has to lean on precision, we're just totally wrecked. [Yudkowsky indicates low disagreement] But there are other possible solutions that don't have to lean on precision, they could exist, and those might not be wrecked. [Yudkowsky indicates high disagreement] [Yudkowsky laughs]

That's where I would expect you would be.

Yudkowsky: Do you want it to be your turn now, to sort of initiate a—

Irving: Sure. I made a list. Let me just pull it up. [laughter] Some useful lists. I would say the chance that we get all the way through this into a good future is about a half. [Yudkowsky indicates very high disagreement] [laughter]

I think there's some question, from our previous chat, about how important it is to model bounded rationality when approximating superintelligence. I think it is probably pretty important to model it. [Yudkowsky indicates very low disagreement]

Oh. Okay. That wrecks one of my fun disagreements. [laughter] We had some discussion about whether, when you're modeling the superintelligent limit, it's more important to model sort of infinite compute, partial alignment or kind of, like, large finite compute. That's why I thought there was a disagreement there, but maybe I misinterpreted that.

Yudkowsky: Hmm. Hard to sort of indicate my level of agreement there—

Irving: Yeah.

Yudkowsky: Without diving into additional details on your viewpoint, I think.

Irving: Okay. So I—

Yudkowsky: Should we sort of keep on going?

Irving: Yeah. Why don't you say something.

Yudkowsky: So I think that there's a sort of pretty fundamental obstacle with respect to imperfect verifiers, the train versus deploy gap. Like the grave difficulty is in sufficiently nailing something before the first time you put it under serious load can wipe out everyone, and that first serious load is very different from all the passively safe testing environments you did. And if you have imperfect verifiers, the current ML techniques are just screwed and will blow up on you, and that does seem pretty fundamental. [Irving indicates low disagreement]

Irving: I think that maybe the important thing to say is I think that we plausibly are in a kind of a non-negligible target world where you can find algorithms which only need to be roughly correct. And then because of sort of training schemes that act kind of recursively on themselves can drive into good equilibria.

And so basically there are two worlds then. One world where no, no, no, you have to get everything precisely right or you're doomed. And that's a world where, I think, we're just totally doomed, and there's nothing we can do in time. We could solve it in enough time. We don't have enough time. And there's another world where there's some decent class of training schemes where if you get kind of a close enough initial start, you will go into a good direction and kind of land well.

Yudkowsky: So if humanity could keep iterating past its first failures, I suspect that the first successful solution would look like what you just described rather than like something very precise. But I also don't think we actually get that. I think that it's imprecise enough that we die. I'm not sure where to register that on the disagreement scale.

Irving: Yeah. I guess I think that you can do some of those… There's a hope of doing some of those experiments in theory land to try to get to proofs and toy models, which are not exact models of the world, but give you enough of a flavor that you can iterate in that space. And that's one of the ways we can get through this.

Yudkowsky: I indicate 50% agreement, meaning that that works 50% of the avenues you try it on. And unfortunately, it would need to be 90% working in order to succeed.

Irving: Sorry, I didn't quite understand that. You mean—

Yudkowsky: So I think you can do it in theory instead of practice half of the time or like 10% of the time if you're in the actual AI lab disaster monkey regime, but like 50% of the time if you're trying what I would consider pretty seriously to get theoretically right. But the theory would need to be right 90% of the time in order to hit the target on this.

Irving: I think that fundamentally there's a… So you're talking about the theory being right with respect to a bunch of domains of model behaviors, correct?

Yudkowsky: Or like slices through viewpoints on what's going on in there. It's not like particular modules of the machine. It's sort of like aspects of the whole thing.

Irving: I think there's at least a reasonable hope that these are super correlated, and so you get— theory that kind of… You get lucky, and it happens to take out kind of… It consistently approximates a bunch of domains all at once.

Yudkowsky: The 50% of them that you can get right are the highly correlated ones, and then the 50% you get wrong have the high independent factors. [Yudkowsky laughs]

Irving: Yeah. So this is why I think that there is… I would place certainly, as we're saying more probability than you on. In fact, you get correlation all the way up kind of to high degrees, and therefore we have some hope of theory getting us through it.

Resolution, singular learning theory and capabilities externalities

Yudkowsky: So I don't know if we should… Whether or not it's wise for us to spend a lot of time talking about this other sector, but to change sectors: Although I'm still currently on the whole net positive on Resolution I think there's— Like, I look at something like singular learning theory, and I'm like, "Gosh, that sure seems more capabilities than alignment to me."

Irving: So if you're trying to do kind of modeling of bounded rationality so that you understand how to model superintelligence, so that you can then do kind of alignment training schemes kind of based on that understanding, I think there's some deep need to have a model of heuristics and how they are learned and kind of what kinds of heuristics are learned. When one heuristic is learned, what's the correlation with one similar heuristic being learned, and so on.

And so there's some sort of understanding of heuristics and generalization, how they emerge over time, and kind of SLT appears to be kind of one of the routes towards this understanding. So that's kind of part of the picture given other parts.

Yudkowsky: That sounds like it feeds into a larger sort of meta-level concern, or disagreement, which might be something like, I'm like, sure, even if they nail… Like nailing singular learning theory would be progress on understanding generalization, which was progress to some degree maybe, toward the team of not entirely human alignment researchers who could nail this. But it's also like in the short term pushing the field of AI generally towards the next step beyond transformers, after which we all die.

Irving: I mostly just think transformers get us all the way to ASI.

Yudkowsky: Well—

Irving: I'm curious where your bar is on this one.

Yudkowsky: Zero to two innovations beyond the level of transformers are required, are… Is what I was saying a decade or… Well, not a decade. Transformers, it felt like a decade [laughter] is what I was saying like four—

Irving: Eight years is nearly a decade—

Yudkowsky: Four years earlier or something. Yeah, so about a decade. [laughter] And now I feel more like it's moved closer to zero to one, in my estimation. But I'm much more sure that it could really get a lot worse than transformers. It might not be required, [Irving indicates low disagreement] but I'm like very sure that trans—

Irving: Oh, gotcha yeah.

Yudkowsky: Yeah. Transformers are n— Yeah. So—

Irving: I would claim the future ASI totally just fits on this hardware. [holds up his smartphone] [Yudkowsky indicates very low disagreement] Yeah. [laughter]

Yudkowsky: Yeah. So I do have some worry that when you do things that look a little more dual use or capability flavored, that they are feeding that much more into capabilities and your alignment team is very close to the bottom of logistic success curve. So you're moving us noticeably closer to the end of the world on capabilities and not very much closer to the saving of the world on alignment. Anytime you study something that's more like 50–50 than like 20–80 on capabilities–alignment.

Irving: Yeah. So I guess maybe one organizational note is that there are people that have… I try to say this in a way that doesn't reveal who the person is, but I have decided to not work with people recently because they're not doing kind of careful analysis of how to be differential here.

I think it is… I basically agree with you that it is hard to do any kind of understanding of heuristics and generalization that doesn't have some degree of capability externality.

I think I don't agree that if you're trying to do it in a way— I think there's a question of how much of the capabilities are coming out of hill climbing and tuning and data and kind of the mechanics that are being kind of run at AI labs. And I place just a ton of the speed is happening due to those factors. [Yudkowsky indicates very low disagreement] And I think we will… Therefore, I expect that the theoretical work is like the default, even though you're intervening on— there's an easier dimension you're intervening on.

But I think that because alignment is going so far behind, I do think that the net effect is most likely positive, but not without a risk of being negative.

Yudkowsky: So I have updated enormously towards AI capabilities progress coming out of people doing alchemy rather than—

Irving: Right.

Yudkowsky: You know,—

Irving: Thinking carefully.

Yudkowsky: Heuristic-based search as opposed to—

Irving: Sure—

Yudkowsky: Like poking-at-things-based search. That's too severe. A bunch of the poking at things is very much heuristic. Like they're not trying random learning schedules, they're trying cosines because computationally simpler learning schedules might be more likely to work than completely random ones. And yet—

Irving: I don't think that's the reason they chose cosine. [laughter] That's an unimportant disagreement to get into.

Yudkowsky: Yeah. Well, it's easy to exaggerate this viewpoint, and I have to work myself not to parody it when I speak it. That said, my massive update towards how much AI progress would be driven by alchemy came with an accompanying cratering of my estimate of how good human institutions would be at the sort of basic progress that could lead to alignment.

Irving: Sure.

Yudkowsky: And I think if you unblock the sort of basic progress that leads to alignment, you're thereby also unblocking the sort of basic progress that leads to doing stuff less alchemically. Like, the reason it's all alchemy is not that alignment research wouldn't contribute to capabilities. It's that humans are so bad at alignment research that it contributes very little to capabilities. [Yudkowsky laughs]

Should anyone do alignment research

Irving: I think this is a reasonable view. I think there are kind of two ways to go. So there's kind of two natural conclusions from this.

One is that, and this is certainly a thing people have kind of proposed to me, that I should not do any alignment research because— well, there are two arguments there. One argument is that it will cause people to not be so worried about things going wrong and so then they'll plow ahead. And the other one is, I think the thing you're saying about, well, just better understanding will give us kind of more speed up.

I think, and then the other… But I find it hard to believe, kind of just in terms of basic heuristics mentally, that that should mean you shouldn't try to solve the problem. So why do I think this? I think this possibly does come back to how big a delta do you expect in the training pipeline required to cause a solution to work out?

If it's like, well, you have some combination of character training plus kind of scalable oversight, plus some form of interpretability and there's a version of that recipe that works, and it's not kind of completely far away from what we have now, then I think in that world, there's a potential for you to make some understanding of kind of general agent heuristics.

It gives you a lens on what classes of things kind of work and don't work. You sort of hand that off to lab alignment teams. They try things. It sort of replicates. You have a combination now of kind of theoretical arguments and kind of empirical validation at low scale, low relative to ASI now. And kind of that gives you a story which you're not all that confident in the answer, but it's better, much better than we have now.

And the question is, like— Somehow that feels like to me it happens prior to causing the paradigm shift in capability research to switch from heuristic poking at things to more principled searching.

Yudkowsky: I'm not sure we should dive into this depth first yet, but I have some theoretical doubts about persona selection and about scalable oversight, and about interpretability continuing to hold up and letting you fix the things that you find with interpretability.

Mech interp and alien concepts

Irving: So for interpretability, I don't yet have a plan to have a mech interp team at Resolution. I was pitching that earlier today. Maybe we will in the future if it's like sufficiently different, but we can skip that one at least.

Yudkowsky: The mech interp teams elsewhere are much less terrible than the poking at it until it misbehaves at alignment and talking about scalable things, teams other places. Like, I do feel there's a legit sense in which that is not the primary place that needs your effort. Like, mech interp has always been healthier than the rest of the field.

Irving: I think talking about personas and scalable oversight as specific topics does seem useful to me. Which one would you prefer to do first, if so?

Yudkowsky: With the side note that my basic objection to mech interp is visibility disappears in the limit, and just because you can see something going wrong doesn't mean you can fix it.

Irving: Maybe it's worth saying that the two issues I have with mech interp currently is that we've tried it for a long time, and we've gotten kind of not that much success.

Yudkowsky: Yeah.

Irving: And then the other one is that, necessarily, ASIs will have crazy alien heuristics. And so the only sense in which you could interpret it would be you have some access to its alien concepts, and then you know the… You understand the [Yudkowsky indicates medium disagreement] expansion process to pull out those concepts into a form that is way, way, way larger than a human could understand. [Yudkowsky indicates medium disagreement]

Yudkowsky: Yeah. I bet if they weren't trying to encrypt that, there'd be a bunch of stuff in there that corresponds to things that you can see in the world.

Irving: To be clear, if they can try to encrypt it, you're totally wrecked. That's a theorem by Vinod [Vaikuntanathan] and Or Zamir.

Yudkowsky: Yeah. Sure. I expect mech interp to break down more because they know we're looking and less because the natural compressed form has zero things in it that map one to one to the ways that humans compress the universe, if that makes sense.

Irving: Sure. I think that's a place where we do disagree, but it probably is a bit hard. I think there's some, like… I have sort of some computational sort of sufficiency model of the world where a sufficiently long computation can in fact… Like, humans can eventually understand most things, but eventually is, like, much longer than the age of the universe. If you just didn't train somebody, you just let them play out the reasoning.

And then if you want to compress things down into some compact form that you can run with only a billion tokens, then you need these crazy alien concepts. But that under this sort of computational, eventually, the enough computation or enough is, like, ridiculous, would be enough, then the process is know how to expand from kind of alien things upwards to much larger traces.

Yudkowsky: It's a pity that this probably isn't our most important disagreement because I bet it would be one of the easiest to make progress on. [Yudkowsky laughs]

Irving: Well, this is the scalable oversight one in some sense.

Yudkowsky: Oh.

Irving: It actually… maybe this is like… yeah, we can choose to go there.

Yudkowsky: But I'm the one who's more optimistic here, so—

Irving: About what?

Yudkowsky: About whether if they didn't know we were looking, their natural way of parsing up the universe would have a bunch of one-to-one correspondences to the way that humans parse up the universe.

Irving: Oh, you think it would have that correspondence?

Yudkowsky: Yeah.

Irving: Sorry, I misinterpreted. I just heard the reverse. I think that that correspondence is going to be very expansive in that you can do the isomorphism in some sense, but it's like it turns one of their tokens into a thousand of our tokens, or one of the tokens into a million of our tokens.

Yudkowsky: Huh. I was expecting it to be the other direction. The human token is a thousand of their tokens, and that's why it's hard to interpret the human token in there.

Irving: I think if you read a professional mathematician's notes, I will not be able to understand them, but there's still… I could ask them to expand it out, and I would understand it then. It's possible that if they read my notes about alignment, you would have to do the reverse expansion, where they need to expand my notes. I think it's… At least a human's kind of domain dependent. I think for an ASI, it's probably not that domain dependent. It's always in one direction.

Yudkowsky: Yeah. I do agree that their proofs look shorter than our proofs, which I think is, like, a sort of different thing than it's like, well, what does a human think a simple proof is? And they need to use, like, 100 of their tokens to describe all the problems and what we think constitutes a simple proof, if that makes sense.

Irving: I see. I think that's them describing a more complicated concept than we are describing in some sense. This is probably unimportant. Yeah. It's a fun topic, I agree. [Irving laughs]

Resolution's theory of impact

Yudkowsky: Just to sort of state meta things clearly, and then we should maybe start diving into depth. I have a theory of change, a theory of impact for Resolution. And it looks like if there's some place on Earth that has 1% of big lab funding, but doesn't have the same pressures on people to exaggerate their positive results, or in some of the places outside the big labs exaggerate their negative results. If you can actually create a place where non-neutral inquiry is not incentivized.

Irving: Yeah.

Yudkowsky: Incentivizing neutral is hard because it's hard to detect neutral. Incentivizing accuracy is hard because it's hard to check accuracy. You can at least avoid incentivizing people stating louder negative results or louder positive results.

Irving: Yeah, so we—

Yudkowsky: Yeah, so—

Irving: We agree on this. [Irving indicates very low disagreement]

Yudkowsky: Yeah. [Yudkowsky indicates low disagreement]

Irving: And I think I also misstated the degree… I stated an insufficiently ambitious version of this in the founding blog post, which you pointed out, and you suggested we're more expansive, and I'll say exactly how. So we don't disagree here. But I think it is… It's a place where I would like feedback to expand and be more ambitious.

So the thing I said in the blog post was, like, we might need to yell, as if we were gonna yell about negative results eventually, which is the wrong viewpoint, and the right viewpoint is, like, you don't… You just constantly spew out what is normally described as both negative and positive results, and you're kind of equally loud about all of them, and you celebrate both kinds and so on. This was a good— this is just your feedback—

Yudkowsky: Yeah.

Irving: Which is good, and so I have tried to relay that internally. I think it's a good principle.

Yudkowsky: Yeah. And so I have the Resolution theory of impact, which is that if you do this, maybe there is eventually a cluster of people who understand why alignment is hard and why the hopeless optimism coming out of the big labs is false, and they're outside MIRI, and they know how to wear suits, and [laughter] they have, like, Professor and Doctor in front of their titles, and they just sort of look and act like academics.

And this produces an additional minor push on politics. Not the same size of push as, like, Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio coming over, but still enough of a sizable push to be worth more than whatever else Coefficient Giving can spend money on. 'Cause what are we gonna do, die with more money? [laughter] But I suspect you have a broader theory of impact than that. [laughter]

Irving: So I should say, though—

Yudkowsky: I would like to get [a disagreement indication].

Irving: I think maybe an important… It's mostly to say, maybe I'll put that, like, here. [Irving indicates medium disagreement]

Yudkowsky: Hmm. [Yudkowsky looks surprised]

Irving: Mostly. So I think part of the neutrality principle is to not prioritize solving the problem versus finding obstacles.

Finding obstacles is only useful if you tell the obstacles to someone. If the eventual thing you find is an obstacle, you either tell it to the labs, they get more paranoid. You're lucky enough that you're in a close to sufficient solution, and their additional paranoia lets them, I don't know, add an actual sandbox or something, or, like, have some monitoring. And so, in that case, plausibly, it's, like, not that far from humans.

Yudkowsky: So, the thing is—

Irving: And so then we sort of… That's where cross-examination comes from, is hiring people to think about the human side, and Beth hired a bunch of humans and did human debates and found flaws and so on.

Yudkowsky: But this is the scholastic method. It is famously insufficient to build a civilization without the experiments occasionally coming up, beating people up and telling them that they are wrong. And if we could do that with superalignment, I would actually be fairly cheerful. Like, if you let us take 50 years, and every year, all the people who had wackily optimistic schemes get beaten up and humiliated, and then a new generation comes in with a new set of wacky schemes, then at the end of 50 years, I think you're pretty good. The problem is to beat up the people who are mistaken that their superalignment scheme would work, then.

Irving: So I think this does—

Yudkowsky: But we can't do that without everybody actually dying.

Irving: I think this does go to, so one is that the scholastic method has given us a number of obstacles to scalable oversight. So, even in my optimistic frame, I think it is broken in several ways already. And so I think that I can make progress against those obstacles in the scholastic frame. The question then is like, how is that plausibly close enough or not? And I think it's quite plausible that it is absolutely not close enough.

Yudkowsky: So an example property your system could require is that with a sufficiently number of diverse rephrasings of piecewise arguments, the noise in the verifiers— the aggregate of the verifiers becomes noisy rather than biased. So, you break down arguments into pieces such that when you apply human verifiers to them or, I bet, GPT-5.6 Terra would be a bunch cheaper. You apply GPT-5.6 Terra to them, it always gives you the truthful and aligned answer in, like, 60% or, like, greater than 51% of cases, like, across the sum of all the diverse ways of phrasing the debates as with pieces being judged by 5.6 Terra or something.

But this to me is an imaginable property and what it boils down to is, if bias, you're screwed. And there— but if magically only noise, then you can win.

Irving: Yeah. So I think that that is, as you say, that's just the bias modeling. And so you have to actually… Sorry, that's just the noise modeling. And so you do in fact have to get a model of the bias and the question is, like, what does that model look like? I think there's something about you have to assume that the structure of all of the reasoning is sufficiently coupled that if you take some field of approximately correct answers and then kind of iterate it through the structure…

I think we're out of time, actually.

Yudkowsky: I think we apparently were out of time eight minutes ago, actually.

Irving: Yeah,—

Yudkowsky: There's— we are now in the middle of a mandatory break. Everyone remaining here is a non-conformist. Let's carry on. [laughter]

Irving: Yeah, I'll just stop as you clearly have to model the bias. I agree with that.

Yudkowsky: Oh, oh—

Irving: I think there's just more hope for that than I think you're expressing.

Yudkowsky: So what we were actually doing is we're building the human bias detectors. So the humans are registering judgments on the steps of the argument and sometimes the human goes like, "Sounds good to me," and GPT-5.8 debiaser fires and is like, "Wrong, human." And GPT-5.8 debiaser is only ever noisy with respect to the true and aligned view of the world, never biased about it.

Irving: That's wrong.

Yudkowsky: Okay.

Irving: I think the debiaser would be, in fact, the big model, not the slightly improved current model.

Yudkowsky: So what we do is we have humans judge a bunch of debates broken down into pieces and then GPT-5.9 debiaser only selects the human judgments that were correct and aligned.

Irving: The overall protocol is going to get this kind of turning it into debiasing, turning it into—

Yudkowsky: Sorry, what is the—

Irving: The overall protocol. The big model plus the overall protocol.

Yudkowsky: Huh. If there were actually a big model protocol like that, why not just put the whole thing into one model or something. What are the humans doing in the system really?

Irving: We don't have the protocol, currently.

Yudkowsky: Anyway, I—

Irving: Think we probably should come to an end.

Yudkowsky: Yeah, yeah.

Irving: Yeah.

Yudkowsky: Well, let's see. We were supposed to do persona selection, scalable oversight. And what was the third thing again? Do you remember?

Irving: I don't remember the third thing.

Yudkowsky: Anybody remember the third thing? Does anyone here have a context window? Sorry?

Audience member: Interp?

Yudkowsky: mech interp, right. And then we decided—

Irving: Oh, I don't think we disagree on that, mech interp.

Yudkowsky: And then we decided to skip that part.

Okay. [Irving laughs] Persona selection. I think you got sort of big tangled messes in there, and a bunch of, like, your training is driving specifically against faithfulness to the naive properties of the persona. Like, if there were ever a Mr. Rogers in there, that part of the system got smashed the first time it was asked questions which Mr. Rogers wouldn't know the answer.

Irving: I think we probably should give people their enforced break. So— that's a much longer conversation. Which would be great fun. [Yudkowsky laughs] But alas.

Yudkowsky: All right.

Audience questions

Break

Moderator: Maybe… Maybe we can do the [unintelligible] break. So everybody stand up.

Audience member: I'm a nonconformist.

Moderator: And Sorry. Thank you. All right, [clears throat] so it's a forced break. So start mulling. And— start mulling. And— if you are a nonconformist, you can stay and the conversation will continue. And yeah, we can have a— We can have… And let's give it up first for the— Thank you. [applause]

Do you want to say something?

Yudkowsky: You're not a very stern enforcer. [laughter]

Irving: We didn't ask for it.

I think we should— if we— the only people have only have, like, 20 minutes of actual break left.

Moderator: Please, you can sit down. Yeah, if you aren't a nonconformist. [laughter]

Audience member: Are we asking questions now?

Moderator: Yeah,—

Irving: I'm happy to talk about personas.

Moderator: They didn't want a rogue moderator, so it's not moderated.

Yudkowsky: Is this on? Okay. Yes. I propose the following rule: everyone has to physically leave the area, and only after returning can the debate continue. Does that sound like we're at least more pretending to have a mandatory break?

Moderator: But this is, like, the approximation to this. Yeah. I've done this before and I… Just, it will work fine. [Yudkowsky sighs] [laughter]

Irving: Did you put the enforced break after our debate for some reason?

Yudkowsky: There are times, not many times, but times when I just feel much more lawful than the people around me. [laughter]

"If not X, we're doomed"

Irving: Maybe one thing to say is, I think that if something like this low-dimensional structure doesn't hold, then we're just totally doomed. [laughter] In the current timescales that are involved.

Yudkowsky: It seems to me that over a lot of my life, I've watched many people come and go saying, "If not X, we are totally doomed, so we might as well assume that X." This turns out to be a very bad argument for X, and usually not X.

Irving: I think this is right, but I do think we have evidence recently for X.

Yudkowsky: Well, that's a very different sort of claim than, "well, we're just doomed if not X," which I suspect that the wrong human argument detector might well trigger on. If it found it inside a debate. [laughter]

Irving: I'm curious if you actually believe what you just said as, like, a b— as, like, not… Like, I would claim that if I'm looking at whether to do kind of governance or not, which is, for example, what I just switched from to, and I see some evidence of, "Oh, here is a thing which there's some evidence for, and if true, I should switch into it. I should switch back into alignment, but like with more probability."

I would claim that's a reasonable heuristic to follow with some degree of strength. I don't know how strong it is. So I don't think I'm making a kind of basic error of rationality there. I'm curious if you agree with that.

Yudkowsky: Well, we're now getting a bit off-topic, and I think we were possibly supposed to take questions at one point or another.

Irving: Oh, good. Questions. What's the questions?

Yudkowsky: But to quickly answer that one, you actually are violating my deontology for how humans should reason, which is that humans should wander about in the world as it appears to be, and have a sort of absolute firewall between their goals and their epistemics, where they're constantly being like, "Well, X or not X," and never of like, "Well, if not X, then we're all screwed, so I might as well assume X."

Like, you just live in the X-less desert and come to terms with it, and keep your eyes open for any path to victory, including those that use not X rather than letting yourself slip sideways into the mental world of X that is more comfortable to live in.

Irving: Just to say, if this evidence hadn't emerged, I would still be working on governance. I think that's a different claim than you're accusing me of making.

Yudkowsky: Possibly. I'm just saying, you never say, "Well, if not X, then…" Pardon me.

Irving: Okay, fair enough. I withdraw that.

Yudkowsky: The way of Eliezer is to never say, "If not X, then we're screwed." It is to say, "Looks like not X, and we're screwed," and then carry on. [laughter]

Is the current world also very bad

Yudkowsky: Person in the back who's had their hand up for a while.

Audience member: Firstly, I just want to say before anyone gets the wrong idea, like— I come from a technical background. I do physics. And also, I am also acutely aware of the fact that if we all die, that is a very bad thing, right?

That could lead us to all die, whether or not the solution is to completely stop that in its tracks. And I do want to make a serious argument—

Irving: Sorry, to be clear, are you just asking if both of us agree that we should stop? 'Cause, like, yeah, definitely. [Irving indicates very low disagreement]

Audience member: Okay. No, no,—

Irving: It's not— You don't have to go… Like, that's not a debate topic.

Audience member: All right. No, no, no, but I do want to raise it because I do feel like it's still important to—

Irving: I've been… Spent the whole week tweeting about this, so we can move on. I think this is not actually, like,—

Audience member: No, but can I actually please—

Yudkowsky: I do have a book on the topic. [laughter]

Audience member: Okay. I want to say the opposite. I want to draw an analogy from the current international development discussions around climate change and where different people from the international community actually sit on it. From my understanding of it—

Yudkowsky: I think I'm going to have to ask you to skip directly to the end of your thesis.

Audience member: Okay. I want… I— You—

Yudkowsky: You have 15 seconds. What is your thesis?

Audience member: The thesis is that whether or not, like, the world if AI takes over will be bad, but the world right now is also very, very bad.

Irving: Okay, I can answer this one very briefly. I think you'll [points at Yudkowsky] probably agree. It doesn't matter how quickly we get to the super good world all that much. It's just not a big term relative to us all dying or not. So slightly delaying getting to the good world—

Audience member: But the thing is that's— It's like, I think— That's very easy for us to say—

Irving: Let's move on, I think.

Yudkowsky: I think we are not presently on course to get a world that is better than the current world, according to me, after taking account that the current world is mildly horrible, that most people in it have not chosen to die and seem to believe themselves to be living lives worth living, and that the current world contains the prospect of happy galaxies, whereas the dead world does not. With all these factors taken into account, I am against the extermination of humanity by ASI and the conversion of many nearby galaxies into states of relatively low worth. Next question.

Stand up and speak loud.

What Resolution wants to automate

Audience member: You say you want to automate things. What do you mean by that, and what do you want to automate?

Irving: So I mostly want to automate— There's some… I think it's important to be… I've spent probably an hour and a half today talking about this. This is good to talk about. With also capability externalities. There's some spectrum of models doing sort of pure theory, like leaf scale proofs, up to generating kind of sublemmas and definitions and so on, up to they're helping people with research taste and choosing directions.

Yudkowsky: Whoa, whoa, whoa. There was a very sharp, very, very sharp jump there between the verifiable part and the hard to verify part.

Irving: I think this is not… This is true eventually, in the sense of, I think the, if you want to go from… So basically what I want to do is automate some lower portion of this spectrum, which I think is mostly kind of below the massive threshold. I do think, though, that if you're kind of trying to produce, like, high— like a… If you're trying to run a hundred agents or a thousand agents doing leaf proofs, several levels up, you have to be automating, them doing kind of sublemma generation and so on. This is auto—

Yudkowsky: Agreed.

Irving: This is verifiable eventually, but on a much larger timescale.

Yudkowsky: Yeah, it's verifiable eventually that you pick the right lemma.

Irving: Correct. Yes. But not immediately and in a weaker sense than the level proofs.

Yudkowsky: Agreed. I do not draw a sharp distinction between that which is immediately verifiable and that which is verifiable an hour or a week later. I do draw a sharp line between, like, only verifiable after the world ends. Like, yeah, dependent on preferences, hard for humans to figure out whether those preferences are actually being respected, et cetera.

Irving: Yeah. So we are trying to automate the stuff that is on the, I would like to think, the correct side of Eliezer's line.

There's an important note there, which is that we also want to think about issues in scalable oversight that could wreck AI labs' plans to automate research. So we have one paper about that from AISI on various ways they could get confused. And I think there is some risk that kind of trying to work on and kind of predict and avoid those obstacles, that has some risk of doing capability acceleration. So—

Yudkowsky: How can it possibly accelerate anything to do with alignment? None of my problems are about staring at a formal theorem and not knowing whether or not that theorem is true. I currently have zero obstacles to alignment that look like that.

Irving: I think, so the obstacles in that paper were sort of labs getting fooled by a whole bunch of experiments with kind of uncertain correlation structure or scalable oversight schemes which kind of fail to bottom out, fail to ex— like you hit basically research taste nodes that you can't expand. And I think if you're trying to kind of understand how scalable oversight will scale up, you do have to think about the obstacles that were in that paper, basically.

Yudkowsky: Sorry, I thought you were talking about automating alignment work and sticking to the verifiable—

Irving: So we don't want to actually do that automation of alignment work, but we do want to think about kind of—

Audience member: Wait, what?

Irving: Issues in scalable oversight that will break, that will cause labs to get kind of false answers out in future and produce like wrong alignment schemes.

Yudkowsky: Oh, yeah, it's the biased verifiers.

Irving: That's right. [laughter]

Audience member: Could you give a few examples of things you do want to automate and a few examples of things you definitely don't?

Irving: Oh, sure. Just like proving Lean theorems, proving prose math theorems, sort of automating simple tasks. It's kind of…

Is any alignment researcher blocked on whether a theorem is true?

Yudkowsky: But who in the entire… Is anyone in this room currently blocked on knowing whether or not some formal theorem is true? Wow. Okay. More than zero hands. What al— Are you working on alignment?

Audience member: Yeah, trying to.

Yudkowsky: So does anyone want to raise their hand and say, like, "By golly, I am working on alignment, and my fundamental obstacle is I do not know whether the following formal theorem is true."

One person. All right.

Audience member: I don't know if it's fundamental, but it's a problem.

Irving: He's admittedly an employee of Resolution. [laughter] Or will be soon.

Yudkowsky: I do not count this against you. Go for it.

Irving: Not currently.

Yudkowsky: Yeah. Let's hear it.

Audience member: Sorry. Give the reason for why don't or not you think it's a blocker.

Yudkowsky: Yeah. Well, what's the question and how is it a blocker to your alignment work?

Audience member: Hello. All right. Hi. Perhaps the easy path of that might be just red teaming. You have an idea, you think it will work, ask for counterexample. So a counterexample can come from, for example, you have a conceptual idea, you try a little bit harder to come out with definitions for that concept in an easier case.

Yudkowsky: Is this setting up the math problem you currently face, or is this you giving an abstract explanation of how a math problem could be relevant?

Irving: It's the abstract one.

Yudkowsky: Okay.

Irving: Just to be— I can say—

Yudkowsky: I was looking for anybody who right now was working on alignment, and by golly, the next thing they need to know is whether or not a certain theorem is true. Like, that's gonna take—

Cole Wyeth: I mean, okay, so it's—

Yudkowsky: Speak up, speak up.

Cole Wyeth: So, okay. For me, there's certainly… it's certainly the case that knowing whether certain mathematical results would be useful for sort of building my intuitions about alignment or something like this. It's not like there's— there's certainly nothing where solving this math problem, I would then have some complete solution to alignment, but there's certain cognitive—

Irving: Maybe it's worth saying that I can answer this question. So I spent literally weeks trying to fix holes in Jonah's proof of a theorem in our prover-estimator debate paper. And I kind of found a bunch of holes in the proof, and then it's like… This is me as chief scientist of AISI. I should not have been doing this, arguably. But it helped lead to Resolution [being founded].

And so I burned kind of weeks on this, find a bunch of holes. Eventually, I kind of gave up in exhaustion. Marshall checked it, and then a couple months later, Jiawei Li found an actual hole that wrecked the whole theorem unless you change the assumptions. And that was like, you had to change the assumptions. It's like a weaker theorem now. And so that actually did lose us kind of like a month, months of time.

Audience member: Was that the evidence you were talking about—

Irving: Say again?

Audience member: Was that the evidence you were talking about earlier?

Irving: The evidence of what?

Audience member: I feel like I have evidence of, like scalable oversight being the, like—

Irving: Oh, I mean, that's one of the problems. It's not the one that Eliezer was complaining about, though. So—

Yudkowsky: Do you want to actually finish the statement?

Cole Wyeth: Yeah. So, okay. So my problem is about whether you can think of the type of rules that certain sort of cautious AIXI variants would be afraid of violating as, like respecting precedent in the sense of avoiding breaking certain laws or so. So sort of like,—

Yudkowsky: I mean, I do suspect that if that's wrong, it's not about a sort of simple theorem. It's about, like, a semi-empirical, like, logical truth, but a very empirical sort of logical truth about whether this very large landscape turns out to have certain statistical properties of, like, if we filter it this way, are the remaining pathways through it all having this property?

Irving: I think it's important to say here that if currently 70% of Cole's time goes to mechanical proof details, and you're saying the important part of the 30%, well, then you can make him three times faster if you speed up the proof details.

Yudkowsky: Sure. I presently think that making alignment researchers three times faster will probably not accomplish all that much, but I guess might get them earlier to the politically useful state where they're pointing at OpenAI and being like, "That won't work." [laughter]

Cole Wyeth: I mean, I can sort of ask this question in math, right? So there are actually a couple of conjectures that I can reduce this to. It's like, that then there's still some difficulty in interpreting. There's some sort of philosophy in interpreting the results, right? But that doesn't mean the results don't matter for—

Yudkowsky: So I think there's a certain legit sense in which, for example, instrumental convergence can be phrased to be a logical truth rather than an empirical truth. Like you take a formal simplicity prior on goal systems, you formally describe a universe. It is now a mathematical truth whether or not instrumental convergence holds, but it's not the kind of mathematical proof that you can get out of Lean if you go harder on your provers. Like, we are now embedding whole universes into the thing we are claiming.

Irving: Wait, sorry. Why can't that go to Lean? That seems— all doable.

Yudkowsky: 'Cause the individual concrete mathematical truths on which you want to take a statistical survey are, like, not tightly correlated enough with each other that you can abstract them away. Like it's, when, one never knows which truth… So, we don't know this for sure, but it could be the case that the Goldbach conjecture is true not for any compact reason, but because it just gets less and less likely to have a counterexample as you keep going, and that the fact that it has no counterexample is just a series of independent truths of increasingly vast probability. And so only its probability of being true is compactly provable, and the statement itself is just never compactly provable.

Irving: Sure, but that's fine. You just kind of assume it's true and move on with your life. Like, those statements you just guess, you run the calculation heuristic argument wise and you just assume them as hypotheses.

Yudkowsky: Yeah. This has been my approach to instrumental convergence. Yeah.

Cole Wyeth: I mean, in this case, it's like part of it's actually like a variant of a coding theorem for a particular complexity. It's not like unachievable to prove sort of thing.

Yudkowsky: Okay. So I think possibly I want to move on from this point and just sort of state that my own stance is something like the 5% of alignment researchers who would be sped up by a factor of three, by access to a theorem oracle, like do not collectively have the power to solve superalignment in time, and that's why I'm not excited, that's why I'm not like breathless with hope of salvation with respect to, like faster proof generation.

Cole Wyeth: Yeah, I agree.

Yudkowsky: Whoever currently has the mic randomly decide who with a hand to give it to. But don't just pick somebody near you 'cause that would be like a overly slow diffusion algorithm.

Audience member: There's another session that's starting in—

Irving: We should probably go.

Moderator: Negative 20 seconds.

Yudkowsky: Oh. Apparently, there's another session in negative 20 seconds. That's—

Audience member: In Rat Park or somewhere else?

Yudkowsky: I'm too lawful. I can't do it.

Irving: We should stop. [applause]

In section ii. of Cat-Belling Problems Yudkowsky briefly mentions this debate and in particular the discussion about scalable oversight.

In Scrying, Modeling, and Nerdsnipe Cole Wyeth (the audience member named above) also mentions this debate and says more about the question of "whether anyone's alignment agenda was actually bottlenecked on solving a math problem".

item.title: Outer space is not consistently big
item.description:
Space is big. You just won't believe how vastly, hugely, mind-bogglingly big it is. I mean, you may think it's a long way down the road to the chemist's, but that's just peanuts to space.

— The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy

When we say "space is big", it's partly meant as a correction to images like this:

where, for simplicity, celestial objects are shown in unrealistically close proximity—like Jupiter is just down the hall from Mars.

As we all know, the planets of the solar system are actually really far apart, even relative to their huge size. In Sweden's 1:20,000,000 to-scale solar system model, Earth and Venus are just ~2 feet in diameter, yet over a mile apart. In other terms, they're several thousand "Earth-widths" apart:

And we all know that's just the start of it: the stars are incredibly far apart. Finland also has a to-scale model of the solar system, but it's 150x more condensed than Sweden's at 1:3,000,000,000.[1] Its model of our sun, Sol, is just ~1.5 feet in diameter.

Its model of the nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is in Australia.[2]

That's even crazier than Earth-Venus, especially considering a "Sun-width" is ~865,000 miles.

So if we keep going bigger, what happens then? What about galaxies?

That image is to scale. If the Milky Way were a typical US suburban home, Andromeda would be a McMansion 3 blocks down the road.[3]

And while many people know that Earth's Moon is not terribly close to Earth:[4]

How many know that the Milky Way's "moon", the Large Magellanic Cloud, is about as close as Earth's Moon is often misleadingly depicted?

There are some interesting implications here; in particular, if your star-faring civilization can colonize the entire Milky Way, you can probably make it over to Andromeda without much more difficulty.[5]

And indeed, you wouldn't stop there either. The next step up from "galaxy" is a "galaxy group", and those can be quite close (relatively speaking) too:

And indeed, Humanity happens to be in a more exurban part of space. If we look at the "nearby" Virgo Cluster[6] ~54 million light-years away (merely 620 Milky-Way-widths), it's quite dense:

If the Milky Way is a typical suburban house, and Andromeda is a McMansion 3 blocks down the street, then the Virgo Cluster is a city center just a 6-mile drive away.[7]

In that sense, space ain't so big after all![8]

If you're curious, here's an interactive widget for checking out distances in relative object-widths. You can see at the bottom that celestial objects' distances in object-widths vary by 7 orders of magnitude;[9] that's what I mean by "outer space is not consistently big".

  1. ^

    Finland does have another one at 1:1,000,000,000, only 50x more condensed.

  2. ^

    Yes there's actually a to-scale model there. It's ~3 inches in diameter.

  3. ^

    Estimates of the size of the Milky Way vary considerably; it's hard to measure from the inside. I am using, for both the Milky Way and Andromeda, estimates of the diameter of what would actually look like part of the galaxy in a typical telescope photo (D25 brightness cutoff), as opposed to how far out outer-disc stars in its gravity extend. (Milky Way: 87,400 light years; Andromeda: 152,000 light years)

    One could argue that actually the "true" diameter of a galaxy ought to include not only outer stars, but also its dark matter halo. If we did that, Andromeda would only be ~1.3 halo-widths away! Considering dark matter is believed to be >90% of the Milky Way's mass, you can understand why it and Andromeda are fated to merge.

    Though it's worth noting that "dark matter halo" is a historical misnomer. Dark matter was first noticed outside of galaxies, but it's now believed that dark matter exists as more of a spherical cloud, densest in the center, where the normal (baryonic) matter is densest too.

  4. ^

    Are you one of today's lucky 10,000 to learn that you could fit every planet in the Solar System between the Earth and the Moon?

  5. ^

    Unless there's something wacky about intergalactic space I'm not aware of? I don't really think it's necessary to resupply at star systems along the way—you only really need to accelerate (and decelerate) once—but even if you needed to, there are stars out in intergalactic space you could use.

  6. ^

    The dense center of the Virgo Supercluster which the Milky Way and Local Group (and M81 Group) are also a part of.

  7. ^

    And the Virgo Supercluster would be the metropolitan area.

  8. ^

    Though I have been informed that "54 million light-years" is a longer distance to walk than 6 miles.

  9. ^

    One could complain that it's unfair to compare "solid" objects like stars to mostly empty objects like galaxies. Fun fact, if we take the "mostly empty" version of a star—a full solar system including its Oort cloud, with a reasonable density cutoff for the Oort cloud—then Proxima Centauri is only ~3 to 17 solar-system-widths away! (we don't know exactly how big or dense Oort clouds are)

item.title: RL Reward-Hack Auditing for Chinese AI Safety
item.description:
TL;DR:
Access to AI safety talent & resources, particularly for labs during training, is sorely lacking in China. We created one of the largest AI safety communities in China, and plan to next start with auditing reward-hacks of unreliable upstream RL environments that domestic data vendors provide to Chinese frontier labs (which induces reward hacking and a whole host of dangerous downstream tendencies).

RL tasks are notoriously prone to exploitation by reward-seeking agents (see examples here, here, and here). In Xiaomi's MiMo v2.6 RL environments that were open-sourced, 2/3 had leaks on Git logs. There's a few clusters of common pitfalls that environments run into, but overall things evolve quickly. From our conversations with employees, CN labs typically don't divert enough people to this particular area, especially since project leads would want senior researchers to work on capabilities research, and because slowing down the development cycle is widely seen as too costly.

The rough shape of our initial solution is an embedded team of staff directly working on identifying & fixing broken environments, working in tandem with the alignment & safety departments within each lab (afaik we estimate that the main Chinese AI players only have 5-10 people per company working on alignment and harm reduction). We are currently in good standing with several labs (our courses' students are often lab employees).

We also plan to produce seasonal (and case-by-case) public reports of specific reward hacking failure modes that we are seeing in RL environments, as well as practical recommendations. This will benefit independent researchers, other evaluators, and data vendors in terms of insights into reducing such failure modes and reducing overall harm. We'd also like to participate in drafting future national and international standards of safety during the training process of AIs.

This is considered by us as a near-term harm reduction strategy for safety & alignment, much like Erowid is to drug safety. It's addressing one of the most pressing current issues that we are seeing direct interest from domestic labs. However, we do have more ambitious plans to expand to areas that more directly address automated alignment in the near future, especially as Chinese companies and the state gradually notice the severity of the issue with near-future warning shots.

item.title: Datasets Determine the Difficulty of Interpretability
item.description:
Recently Goodfire has come out swinging with two posts indicating that neurons in transformers are "more interpretable than previously assumed", or simply "already clean". In the "Neurons as Interpretable Basis" post they offer three reasons for this claim:

  • First, neurons are already functionally sparse - pruning 92 % of the weakest MoE neuron activations only increases the loss by 2.9%
  • Second, the role of a neuron can be split into different "computational functions". Effectively, we can name the contexts in which a neuron fires, and assign reasons to those firings. Most neurons only have one context-reason grouping.
  • Finally, we can produce automated natural language explanations of neuron firings that are predictive of their behaviour.

First, I would like to congratulate them for their detailed work and breakdown, complete with well-designed graphics. I found the work interesting and very well thought through. It is a shame that we have no idea if these techniques apply to lab models with non-public architectures, but I think it is fairly reasonable to say that at least some of this work is transferable directly (perhaps until a fully recurrent architecture is the norm instead of looped transformers).

Next, I would like to consider the original motivations for interpretability. In A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits, Elhage et al. write:

Transformer language models are an emerging technology that is gaining increasingly broad real-world use, for example in systems like GPT-3, LaMDA, Codex, Meena, Gopher, and similar models.  However, as these models scale, their open-endedness and high capacity creates an increasing scope for unexpected and sometimes harmful behaviors.  Even years after a large model is trained, both creators and users routinely discover model capabilities – including problematic behaviors – they were previously unaware of.

One avenue for addressing these issues is mechanistic interpretability, attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by transformers, similar to how a programmer might try to reverse engineer complicated binaries into human-readable source code.  If this were possible, it could potentially provide a more systematic approach to explaining current safety problems, identifying new ones, and perhaps even anticipating the safety problems of powerful future models that have not yet been built.

From this we can intuit a rationale to engage in mechanistic interpretability research based on several factors:

  • Open-endedness: Transformer models can engage in novel behaviour in unexpected situations, including generalisation to novel domains outside of training data.
  • Emergence of problematic behaviour: Some of these novel behaviours are problematic and unexpected.
  • Explainability: Interpretability allows us to explain why these problematic behaviours occur.
  • Anticipation of future issues: Interpretability allows us to potentially predict the existence of problematic behaviours before they are discovered "in the wild", including in future models.

With this in mind, the distribution of prompts and documents from which Goodfire draws its conclusions is of paramount importance. The power of a theory lies not in its ability to explain the well-known, but in its ability to offer counterfactual predictive power in novel situations (For interpretability, a simple test would be whether the proposed explanation or prediction of model behaviour is more informative than just reading the prompt). Therefore, I would be excited to know what the dataset of prompts and documents Goodfire used to derive its results contains.

In addition, here are some categories of texts I would be particularly interested to see when testing if interpretability techniques generalise:

  • In context learning: Prompts which consist of novel patterns or sequences that must be learned in-context. For example, create a randomised POMDP, give the transformer a list of recent observations, then ask it to predict the next observation.
  • Gibberish: Nonsense data with random words or phrases strung together.
  • Glitch tokens or sequences: The equivalent of "solidgoldmagikarp", spiralism prompts, "see the below" etc.
  • Hors-text: System prompts, constitutions, soul documents etc. In general, anything that has been given "synthetic emphasis" during mid-training or post-training.
  • Jailbreaks and malicious prompts: This is probably self explanatory.

I am excited to see what these experiments reveal!

item.title: Ralph Page on Live Music
item.description:
Ralph Page was a very influential dance caller who published Northern Junket, a square dance magazine. This was "square dance" in the broad sense, before the club and trad communities divided, and while he came from a strong live music tradition he was living through the transition to recorded music.

I looked through the Northern Junket archives to see his perspective on live music, and I came across a few passages that show the wave of the contra dance revival sweeping across New England in the early 1970s.

In Vol 9 No 8 (1969), Page is writing about live music as something so rare that most haven't danced to it. An evening dance in Cambridge with live music is an exciting exception:

How long has it been since you danced to good live music? I'll imagine that seventy-five percent of the club dancers in this country have never had that pleasure. What a pity! It might be a way of keeping your group interested in dancing. Certainly nothing would be lost if every square dance club started an orchestra to play for their parties. At first perhaps they could play but for one set of dances. So what? It would be a start. And as their repertoire increased I am sure that interest in that particular club would increase in like manner.

I had the privilege of calling for a special recently at the Cambridge, Mass. YWCA, sponsored by the Taylors. Live music was the feature of the evening. Elise Nichols and Walter Lob played their fiddles and were more than ably 'seconded' by Marianne Taylor at the piano. What wonderful music they played! As the dance drew to a close they were given a thunderous ovation from the big crowd. They deserved it. The party was worth attending just to listen to such tunes as Massai's Favorite, Cincinnati Hornpipe, Pig Town Fling and Haste To the Wedding.

Time is getting short because good fiddlers are getting to be as scarce as hen's teeth. There is little incentive for violinists to learn the old tunes. It would be interesting to learn of any clubs that are trying to keep live music from becoming a lost art as far as square dancing is concerned.

Here he's commenting on it being rare, but not getting into the why. A couple issues later in Vol 9 No 10 (1969) he blames economics:

Soon the entire country was flooded with square dance recordings, and the necessity of using records was brought on by the high price that musicians ask to play for a dance.

Three years later, in Vol 11 No 1 (1972), it's a very different story:

One of the most heartening things about the just ended dancing season is the increased use of live music. Many of the musicians are college students or in some cases, teenagers. And these young people are GOOD! Sannella, of Lexington, Mass. tells me that he has had far more requests for dances with an orchestra than ever before. Perhaps the heyday of canned music for dancing is over and done with.

The C.D.S. Drop In evenings have I believe, always insisted on live music at their Thursday night parties, Dick Davis uses live music almost entirely. Dick Leger (for my money the best caller in the country) frequently calls to an orchestra. Let's not get too ecstatic or go overboard with the idea but at least the road back has begun it seems.

Many of the young people getting interested in square and folk dance music, are trained musicians. That bodes well for the future. The old-time orchestra was good enough to play an hour-long concert of "heavy" music, before the dancing began. Some of these young folks could do that now, and the rest of them, will be able to within a very few years. God speed the day!

Perhaps some of the square dance clubs that are just barely hanging on could make a come-back if they could: find 3-4 of the members who would be willing to play for an evening's dancing once in a while. Who knows? Stranger things have happened!

And then a few months later in Vol 11 No 4 (1973) he writes:

There is a young man here in middle New England who is leading many weekly public dances. His average attendance is between 200 and 300 young college-aged and younger dancers. His program is at least 75 percent contra dances with some English country dances quite often, and always a few of the round dances that have been danced here for a couple of dance generations, such as Gay Gordons, The Roberts, Road to the Isles etc. His success is not something that has happened overnight; it has been growing for at least five years. He MUST be doing something right!

While this doesn't mention live music, this is pretty clearly Dudley Laufman who would have been playing fiddle or accordion while calling.

I would like to go back through more sources and pull more of this history together, but it's interesting to see how sudden the reversal was. Or maybe he's talking about two different scenes here, with club squares pulling apart from traditional contras and squares, and this is not as sudden as it looks?
